sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Mutapa is the Shona empire that kept its mines: in our history a Mutapa king ceded them to Portugal in 1607, and here he didn't. Sixty years later his heirs rule the richest state on the Indian Ocean, run it like a counting house, and power it with a metal no one else knows how to use.

**The one thing to remember:** Mutapa isn't a hidden kingdom; it's an open one with a secret. Everyone trades with it, and no one can copy it. In 1668, the people whose job it is to notice have noticed.

> **Further in:** what Mutapa sells is not what it has.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
A high plateau, mostly over a thousand meters up: not jungle or endless savanna, but open woodland that goes bare in the dry season.

- **Seasons.** Cool and dry (April to early August, with frost on the high plateau from mid-May), hot and dry (to October), and the rains (November to March), which decide the year.
- **The granite country.** *Kopjes*, granite domes and boulder hills, stud the plateau; their natural slabs built Great Zimbabwe without mortar.
- **The Great Dyke.** A ridge of ultramafic rock runs about 550 km down the country's spine. Only a few specialist plants grow on it, which is how a druid found the platinum.
- **The lowlands.** Tsetse fly and malaria in the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys kill cattle and strangers. The plateau states sit in the healthy high country, and anyone after Mutapa's gold crosses the fever country to reach it.
- **The coast.** Sofala's harbor, mangroves, the Sofala Bank fishery, and the monsoon, which blows ships north half the year and south the other half.
- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age; the coldest decades, 1690 to 1740, are still ahead.

> *"Everyone who comes up from the coast expects Africa to be hot. Then the first frost comes, and they start asking where to buy a Mutapan stove."* (a Sofala innkeeper)

> **Further in:** in our history, from the late 1660s to about 1680, locusts, smallpox, measles and plague emptied the Mutapa lands, and wild animals moved back into abandoned villages. Here the healers blunt it, but they are few, and it still comes.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
On paper, a king.

- **The crown.** Mutapa has a royal line, anointed in the old way. In our history Mukombwe took the throne around 1663. He keeps it: history keeps its shape where magic didn't bend it.
- **The merchant houses and the scientists** hold the real power; the houses run the king. Whichever house has his ear steers Mutapa, and right now it's the shewstone house, which is why the king wants the whole world to see Mutapa's glory.
- **The royalty** knew a good thing when it saw one, but isn't sure it's the right steward for what it found. Neither is anyone else.
- **The House of the Bird**, named for Great Zimbabwe's soapstone birds, is the bank. It prices gold by the coast's Arab *mithqal* and learned credit from the Gujarati merchants who finance much of the ocean's trade.
- **The spirit mediums.** A Shona king's legitimacy runs through the royal dead, who speak through human mediums. Later sources call these spirits *mhondoro*, "lions," and their mediums *svikiro*. In Euphonia the spirits are real.
- **The Cape's own people.** Mutapa rules the Khoekhoen of the Cape the way Shona kings have always ruled neighbors (Scott): the chiefdoms nearest the harbor are tributaries, bound by cattle Mutapa lends them (a borrower of the king's cattle is the king's man), by the new fire lit each reign from the king's own, and by a tax on every trade. Further out, the Cochoqua and the Chainouqua take Mutapa's terms when it suits them and a Dutch or English captain's when it doesn't. The San hold the mountains and the dry country, in no one's ledger.

> **Further in:** in the 1590s a Portuguese friar watched a possessed man at a king's royal graves speak in the dead king's voice, asked about war, famine and rain. A merchant house can buy a minister. It can't buy a dead king.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Mutapan magic is artifice, and it runs on platinum. It isn't stronger than other magic. It's better made.

- **The catalyst.** Platinum isn't consumed, so a Mutapan device runs for years where a European enchantment burns out. It turns raw magic into current, doesn't corrode, and calibrates: one device behaves exactly like the next. That means workshops instead of lone geniuses, and interchangeable parts a century early.
- **Small work for anyone, big work for the trained.** A Mutapan lamp lights itself for whoever owns it; a weapon, a flight pack or an Arc Gun needs a trained artificer, a **Mhizha** (Shona for a master craftsman, now the name of the whole art).
- **Mutapa doesn't sell the big work,** and the small work drifts out of calibration, so a foreign owner eventually needs Mutapan hands to retune it.
- **The curiosity.** Abroad, the small devices are the fashionable rarity of the day: the lamp in a Viennese drawing room that tells guests how far its owner's reach extends.
- **Shewstones.** Europe's speaking stones are sperrylite, a platinum mineral: tin-white, mirror-bright, never large, full of arsenic. They come from Mutapa, and the king wants every court to have them; his great artificer and his spymaster think it's the most dangerous thing he's done.

> **Further in:** the platinum came to Mutapa through a druid reading the plants on the Dyke. Nobody has asked what else the plants know.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Southern Africa's Hidden go by their own names. Most of the record is 19th- and 20th-century, projected back; the royal mediums are the exception.

- **The water-takers.** Shona *njuzu*, pool spirits, take a person under, feed them mud and raw fish, and send some back as healers if the family doesn't mourn: in Euphonia, the calling of an **Oceanus Revelator**.
- **The river people.** In Xhosa tradition, one called by the river is taken to a snake-guarded enclosure underwater, where a half-fish old woman embodies the clan's ancestors; they return on the third day, in white clay.
- **The wanderers.** A *shave*, the spirit of someone who died far from home, chooses a host and gives a skill: hunting, healing, dancing, fighting. Unlike an ancestor, it can be refused.
- **The small people.** The Zulu *abatwa* are tiny, touchy hunters of the grass and anthills, with fixed rules for greeting them.
- **The bargain.** *Umamlambo* is a river woman or snake bought for wealth and paid for with a parent's life.
- **The Cape's Hidden.** The Khoekhoe Water Snake that keeps the springs, and the rain-animals of the San, the bull and the cow of the rain: here, Hidden on the land's own terms.
- **The new border.** Mutapa's cities are growing fast into country that was always someone else's, and on their edges modern artifice meets the oldest things in the land. The Wild Hunt rides here too, under its own names.

> **Further in:** the Rain Queens of the Lobedu, far to the south, trace their line to a princess who fled Mutapa with the power to make rain.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
The freeze-frame:

- **The red alert.** Every court's minister of magic has run the numbers on Mutapan curiosities and concluded that Mutapa is about to vault the magical gap entirely. Their intelligence services are moving.
- **The platina.** The same metal lies in Spain's Chocó, in New Granada, and Spain dumps it in the river. Whoever works that out first changes the world.
- **The Cape.** Mutapa holds Hoerikwaggo, its town under Table Mountain: the gate every European fleet must pass to reach the Indies, and the great flashpoint.
- **The cattle.** The Cape's winter rains defeat the plateau's summer crops, so a Mutapan Cape lives on ships and on Khoekhoe cattle, and the herders know it: they trade the old and the barren and keep the breeding stock.
- **The go-between.** A Khoekhoe woman about twenty-five years old, raised in the harbor town, speaks four languages and is the most useful person at the Cape to four powers. In our history Krotoa lost her husband and her place in 1668.
- **The Rozvi.** In our history a herder, Changamire Dombo, got land around 1670, gathered followers he called the Rozvi, and rose against the crown. Here that break hasn't come.

> **Further in:** in our history, Dombo rose in the same years the plagues were emptying the Mutapa lands.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The apprentice in London.** A Mutapan artificer has taken an English apprentice, and every court in Europe wants to know what he's teaching.
- **The Cape.** A Dutch fleet, an English one, and a Mutapan harbor master who cares only whether a ship pays.
- **The far chiefdoms.** A Cochoqua chief takes an English captain's muskets and Mutapa's cattle in the same month, and both think he's theirs.
- **The man from Sofala.** A Khoekhoe interpreter trained at Mutapa's ports comes home angry about the grazing, and knows exactly how Mutapan arms fail.
- **The ship with the fever.** Smallpox, in our history, reached the Cape on a ship in 1713 and killed most of the Khoekhoen near it. A ship from Sofala could bring it decades sooner, and whom Mutapa's healers treat first decides what the Cape becomes.
- **The painter.** In the mountains a San painter is putting Mutapa's ships on a rock wall.
- **Who governs?** A merchant house's quarrel with a royal medium, and a dead king with opinions.
- **The great artificer's choice.** Whatever he decides, someone will try to stop him.
- **The Monsoon Road** starts here: a ship, a cargo of curiosities, and an ocean of people who want to see inside one.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
Western Europe is four crowns that have just stopped killing each other over religion and started competing over everything else: ships, companies, credit, colonies, magic. Each has a minister of magic and licenses it; in 1668 each has just learned that it is behind.

**The one thing to remember:** in Western Europe magic is a state asset, and the crime isn't magic, it's unlicensed magic. Whoever writes the license holds the power, so a license is a weapon, and the Great Game is fought with them.

> **Further in:** there is no divine right in Euphonia, unless a particular king has some divine ability.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Not one great forest: the lowlands were cleared centuries ago, and what woodland is left is managed, coppiced, or royal hunting forest under its own law.

- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age is at its depth (1668 sits inside the Maunder Minimum). Hard winters come in clusters; the Thames froze in four winters between 1649 and 1666.
- **The plague's tail.** London's Great Plague was 1665–66, and Basel's last outbreak is running now. Healing magic tempers every epidemic, but healers, druids and clerics are not common, so they blunt an outbreak and can't stop one.
- **The fens.** Investors and Dutch engineers are draining England's Fens; the fenmen, who fish and fowl there, break the dikes, and the drained peat shrinks and floods again.
- **The uplands.** Highland Scotland, Wales and western Ireland are open grazing. Wolves are gone from England but survive in the Highlands and Ireland.
- **Ireland**, the empire nearest home, is being remapped: Catholics held about 60% of its land before Cromwell's conquest, and the Down Survey (1656–58) mapped what was forfeited.

> *"The Thames froze again. The printers set up on the ice, and someone sold a Mutapan stove to warm the booth. It cost more than the press."* (a London stationer)

> **Further in:** the Fens are being drained for profit, and the fenmen say the marsh had other tenants before the investors came.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Scott's rule: a court's read on magic follows who controls its church. Crowns that own their churches absorb magic; church-run states regulate it.

- **France absorbs.** Louis XIV has ruled in person since 1661; Colbert runs finance, manufactures and the colonial companies. His crown-salaried Académie royale des sciences (1666) meets privately in the King's Library, without statutes. The *cabinet noir* reads the post; the Huguenots still have the Edict of Nantes. The Académie tests and recommends; the minister is Colbert, for whom magic is one more manufacture, and his clerks keep the register of licenses.
- **England absorbs.** Charles II, restored in 1660, keeps an alchemical laboratory and inherits John Dee's legacy: the shewstones are how the crowned heads talk. The Royal Society (1660) is a self-funded gentlemen's club, not a state body; Scotland's Kirk is a rival source of legitimacy. No named office: magic belongs to a committee of the Privy Council, which borrows the Royal Society's Fellows when it needs an expert eye.
- **Spain regulates.** The last Spanish Habsburg, Charles II, is a child king under his mother's regency (general knowledge, not in the research files). The Inquisition's *Suprema* has required material evidence in witchcraft cases since 1614, and the crown has defaulted on its bankers again and again. The *Suprema* issues the license and the crown taxes it: in Spain, a practitioner answers to the Inquisition first.
- **Portugal** is independent again under the Braganzas, after sixty years under Spain's king. It has lost Malacca and Colombo to the Dutch and, in Euphonia, Sofala to Mutapa. Catherine of Braganza's dowry gave England Bombay and Tangier.
- **The Dutch Republic is pragmatic,** and burned England's fleet in the Medway in 1667. The States General and the provinces rule, not a king. Its weapons: the Amsterdam Wisselbank, whose bank guilder is Europe's unit of account; the VOC and WIC, private companies with the right to make war; and presses that print banned books under false imprints.

> **Further in:** in Euphonia the VOC never built its station at the Cape. Mutapa holds it. At Mauritius, which the Dutch resettled in 1664, and, when they must, at Mutapa's harbor under Table Mountain, where they pay like everyone else.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Western wizardry follows the Children of the Emerald Tablet, Hermetic schools entrenched in the universities. The natural philosophers came out of the same programs, and the Children lead the charge against them.

- **The minister of magic.** Every government has one; its job is the license: who may practice, teach, sell and heal. Grant it to a friend, revoke it from a rival, and the rival is a criminal.
- **The witch hunts** matter because there are real witches. England has hanged at least 500; Scotland has tried 3,837, 84% of them women (its last great panic was 1661–62); Spain's Inquisition braked the burning after 1614. A sorcerer erupting in a crowded town is part of why the anti-magic people are the way they are.
- **The Romani** are hunted as vagrants more than as witches. France sends Romani men to the galleys (1666); Spain has banned the word *gitano*, Romani dress and the Romani language (1633); England has hanged Romani under its Egyptians Acts. Fortune-telling is charged as fraud. In Euphonia, too, the old accusation that they steal children is false: when a child vanishes, look to the Hidden.
- **Cunning folk** are literate, often book-owning, and mostly not the hunts' targets; they practice the licensed magic out past the institutions' reach.
- **Clerics.** Holiness works for anyone actually holy. Catholic and Protestant clerics work exactly the same: for all the bloodshed and rancor, it doesn't matter a whit.

#### Lanternhall

**Lanternhall**, in Basel, is Europe's first teaching hospital of its kind and the first serious rival to the Church's healing. Basel sits where the Swiss Confederation, Alsace and the Empire meet; Paracelsus taught there in 1527 and burned Avicenna's *Canon*.

- Before it, the Church held the only healing that worked, at the price of conversion; charging for it was one of Luther's 95 Theses. Protestants heal for free, but only their own. Both Churches oppose upstart wizards who think they can replicate the Savior's work.
- Hedge witches have the same magic as Lanternhall's and get no respect. The Islamic world, with its long hospital tradition, wonders what the fuss is about.

> **Further in:** Basel's last plague (around 1665–70) killed the young poor; the mass grave under the old plague hospital averages seventeen years old. There were never enough healers.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Western Europe's Hidden go by many names, and people avoid saying any. The 1668 evidence is court records and a few believers' treatises; most "folklore" was collected in the 19th century.

- **The Good People.** The Good Neighbors, the Gentry, the People of Peace; in Irish, the *aos sí*, the people of the mounds. Farmers leave Ireland's 45,000 surviving ringforts, their houses, unplowed. Robert Kirk (1691–92) called them "of middle nature between Man and Angel."
- **In the witch trials,** a healer says her skill came from the fairies, and the court recasts the fairies as the Devil. In 1662 Isobel Gowdie said she had feasted with the fairy king and queen, seen elf boys making arrowheads, and learned a charm to become a hare.
- **"Seely"**, an old Scots word for blessed or lucky, names kinds of fairy, not a government; the two-court model is attested only from 1783 and 1819.
- **The taken.** Fairies take infants, and new mothers to nurse fairy children, and leave a sickly substitute.
- **Goblins** are the Hidden's soldiers, or something like it; that's why England has them.
- **The Wild Hunt** rides out of the Bordermarches under local names: Herne the Hunter, the Gabriel Hounds of the north, Gwyn ap Nudd and the *Cŵn Annwn* in Wales, the *Mesnie Hellequin* and *le Grand Veneur* in France, Arthur in Brittany, the *hueste antigua* in Castile. ("Wild Hunt" itself is Grimm's term, from 1835.)
- **Protections.** Iron in the cradle and the doorway; St John's wort and yarrow against them. Hawthorn and foxglove are theirs, and harming them invites revenge.
- **Hidden Killers** patrol the rural villages here as everywhere.

> **Further in:** a fairy grandmother is a family story in one country and a witch-trial accusation in the next. Old families on both sides of the Channel have reasons to keep the licensing office friendly.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
The freeze-frame:

- **The red alert.** Every court's minister of magic has run the numbers on Mutapan curiosities and concluded that Mutapa is about to vault the magical gap. Their intelligence services are moving.
- **The platina.** Spain has been throwing away the metal Mutapa runs on, in the Chocó, but its court has worked it out: the Queen Regent went through a gate to New Granada to see it, and foreign agents saw her go (Scott, 2026-10-26). If the Chocó is easy to take, England and France need only a fleet.
- **The Treaty of Lisbon.** Spain recognizes Portugal's independence, and Portugal recognizes Ceuta, loyal to Spain since 1640, as Spanish.
- **Aix-la-Chapelle.** France ends the War of Devolution keeping twelve Spanish Netherlands towns; in July Versailles, still the king's pleasure house, holds the Grand Divertissement royal.
- **The companies.** The English East India Company takes over Bombay. The first Hudson's Bay voyage sails. Barbados, under the first English slave code (1661), sends England 80% of its Caribbean sugar.

> **Further in:** in our history, England and France attack the Dutch Republic together four years from now, in 1672.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The missing child.** A village blames a Romani family for a child the Hidden took, and the magistrate sits on Monday.
- **The apprentice in London.** A Mutapan artificer has taken an English apprentice, and every court in Europe wants to know what he's teaching.
- **A license revoked.** A court wizard loses his license over a court quarrel and becomes, overnight, an outlaw with a court wizard's knowledge.
- **The Chocó question.** Which crown sends the first fleet, and under what flag.
- **Lanternhall's next graduate** goes home to a country whose Church hasn't licensed her.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
East of France and south of the Alps, nobody is in charge. The Empire is hundreds of territories under an elected emperor. Poland–Lithuania elects its king, and one deputy can void a parliament. Sweden has a regency, Venice councils, Italy Spain, the Pope and a few dynasties. Russia is the exception, and it is splitting over how to make the sign of the cross.

**The one thing to remember:** where authority is divided or weak, the witch hunts burn. With no single hand on the license, every prince, bishop and village court decides for itself what counts as unlicensed magic.

> **Further in:** the Empire's largest witch hunts were in lands ruled by bishops.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The forests that are left.** The big forests are here: the German uplands, the Alps, the Carpathians, Poland–Lithuania and Russia, and even these are being cut for ships, charcoal and mine props.
- **The Black Forest** is being floated down the Neckar and the Rhine to Dutch shipyards and canal piles, on rafts over 300 m long with crews of up to 500. Its oaks are disappearing.
- **The scars of the war.** The Thirty Years' War (1618–48) killed 4.5 to 8 million, mostly civilians, mostly by disease and hunger; some German regions lost over half their people, counting those who fled.
- **The Alps.** Summer pastures and mule passes. Glaciers are advancing on farms, and villages answer with processions and exorcisms.
- **Venice's lagoon** is always silting up. The Republic diverts whole rivers to keep it water.
- **The plains.** Sand, heath, bog and rye from the Netherlands to Russia; to the south-east, the Hungarian plain on the Ottoman frontier, and the Pontic steppe of Cossack, Tatar and Nogai herds.
- **Animals.** The last aurochs died in a Polish royal forest in 1627. Wolves are common; bears are in every mountain range and the east.
- **Disease.** Plague is ending (Venice's last was 1630–31). Healing magic tempers every epidemic, but healers, druids and clerics are not common, so they blunt an outbreak and can't stop one.

> **Further in:** a Black Forest fir felled in 1668 can end up as a pile under an Amsterdam canal house. Nobody asks the forest.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Empire.** An elected Habsburg emperor in Vienna, eight electors, and since 1663 a permanent Imperial Diet at Regensburg, a congress of envoys. Each prince chose his territory's religion, now frozen as it stood in 1624. One per prince: each prince licenses magic in his own lands, as he chose their religion. Vienna's minister answers for the Habsburg lands, and the Diet argues about the rest.
- **The Habsburg frontier.** Hungary is split three ways: Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary, and Transylvania, an Ottoman tributary guaranteeing four religions and leaving out the Orthodox. The Military Frontier is a belt of armed refugee colonists, many Vlach and Serb, holding land for permanent border service.
- **Venice.** The doge has little power; the councils have it. The Council of Ten runs security and espionage, with three State Inquisitors, "lion's mouth" boxes for written denunciations, and a cipher bureau a century ahead of its rivals. Venice sells noble rank to pay for the Cretan War.
- **Rome.** The papacy's prestige rests on faith, not power at the great game table. The Holy Office has prosecuted learned magic and astrology since 1586, and the Index bans the books: officially against magic, privately scholarly. Quietly, yes: the Holy Office keeps scholars who study what it bans, on the grounds that someone must.
- **The rest of Italy.** Medici Tuscany is scholarly, though its Accademia del Cimento closed in 1667. Naples, Sicily and Milan have Spanish viceroys.
- **Sweden**'s empire of 2.5 million people is governed by a regency for the boy king Charles XI; its former queen, Christina, abdicated, converted, and lives in Rome.
- **Denmark–Norway** became one of Europe's most absolute monarchies under the Lex Regia of 1665, and lives on the Sound Dues, a toll on every ship through the Øresund.
- **Sápmi**, the Sámi north, is taxed by Sweden, Denmark–Norway and Russia, sometimes all three in one winter. Sweden's church is pressing in: a school at Lycksele since 1632, drums seized, noaidi questioned. At Nasafjäll the crown forced Sámi to haul silver ore until the mine burned in 1659, and many fled to Norway.
- **The Romani of the east** live under other rules. In Wallachia and Moldavia they are enslaved, owned by princes, boyars and monasteries; in Hungary and Transylvania the diets pass no laws against them and protect their smiths and their voivodes.
- **Poland–Lithuania** elects its king. The *szlachta*, about a tenth of the people, rule through the Sejm, where one deputy's veto can void a session.
- **Poland's wounds.** The Deluge (1655–60) cost a third of the population; the Truce of Andrusovo (1667) gave Russia left-bank Ukraine. South lie the Cossack Hetmanate, in the years called the Ruin, and the Crimean Tatars' slave raids.
- **Russia.** Tsar Alexei rules from Moscow. The 1666–67 councils deposed Patriarch Nikon but anathematized the old rite, and the Old Believers would rather burn than change how they cross themselves. Siberia runs on river forts and forced fur tribute, against continuing resistance; epidemics have killed up to four-fifths of some Tungus and Yakut groups.

> **Further in:** the only platinum deposit that could match the Great Dyke is at Norilsk, in Arctic Siberia, where Russian fur traders and tribute collectors are just arriving.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **The hunts.** Germany has over half of Europe's witch trials, the worst in prince-bishoprics like Trier, Würzburg, Bamberg and Eichstätt (almost 300 burned in 1617–31). Torture produced chains of accusation; a Jesuit's anonymous *Cautio Criminalis* (1631) attacked the procedure and helped end the trials in Mainz. Here the hunts find real witches, and also anyone a neighbor names.
- **Prague's legacy.** Rudolf II's court kept Tycho, Kepler, Dee and Kelley under one roof, and imprisoned Kelley when his alchemy failed. In Euphonia, their crystals worked: the shewstones began there.
- **Learned spirits.** Agricola, founder of mineralogy, wrote up the mine spirits as mining science; Paracelsus classified the elementals (gnomes, undines, sylphs, salamanders), and in 1668 his book is widely read.
- **The night battles.** In Venetian Friuli the caul-born *benandanti* said their spirits left their bodies on the Ember Days to fight witches over the harvest, armed with fennel stalks. The Inquisition slowly turned them into witches.
- **The ladies from outside.** In Spanish Sicily, healers joined the *donne di fuora*, fairy companies under a Prince; the Inquisition mostly treated them as deluded.
- **Kabbalists** are wizards, Envoy warlocks, or both. A golem walks the Venetian ghetto after dark.

> *"The bishop's court wanted names. I gave them the woman who sold me a charm that worked. They burned her, and I still have the charm."* (a Franconian miller)

> **Further in:** in Venice, the Inquisition drowned its condemned rather than burning them.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Every part of this region has its hidden folk, but the 1660s record is thin, mostly church condemnations and trials; the detail is 19th-century. Slavic, Alpine and Scandinavian customs are alive and contradict one another.

- **The mine folk.** Kobolds help and hinder in houses and mines; Agricola's *Bergmännlein* look like old miners, laugh, throw pebbles, and can lead a miner to silver. A troublesome ore, *kobelt*, was named after them, and cobalt is named for it.
- **The wild folk.** The hairy *wilder Mann*; the Tyrolean *Saligen Fräulein*, "blessed maidens"; Rübezahl, the weather spirit of the Riesengebirge, in print from 1662.
- **The leshy** is the master of a Slavic forest: as tall as the trees inside it and as short as the grass outside. The forest's edge is the edge of his power, which makes the village edge literal here.
- **The rusalka** is a water spirit, the soul of a drowned girl or unbaptized child, who dances in the birches at the start of summer; join the ring and you dance to death.
- **The domovoi** lives by the oven, and a family moving house has to invite him along.
- **The North.** Underground people, the forest *huldra*, the fiddling *näck*, the farm's *tomte* (mostly collected later).
- **The Wild Hunt** rides out of the Bordermarches as Wodan's *Wütendes Heer*, led by Holda in the north and Perchta in the south, or by the cursed huntsman Hackelberg; in Norway it's the *Åsgårdsreia*.
- **Where the edge doesn't fit.** The steppe herders and the Sámi reindeer herders of Sweden's north have no village edge, and their Hidden don't wait at one. The Sámi underground people, the *gufihtar*, keep herds of their own and move with the seasons too. They take children, and a taken child who refuses their food comes home. (unverified: when the gufihtar lore was first written down)
- **The Black Forest** has fae-touched giants out of Grimm.

> **Further in:** at Blåkulla the children said they were carried away at night to a feast inside a hill. The theology was the Devil's, but the shape is the Hidden's.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
The freeze-frame:

- **The Blåkulla panic begins.** In Härjedalen, Märet Jonsdotter's trial starts rumors that witches are carrying children to a sabbath at Blåkulla. In our history the panic runs eight years and kills dozens, children among them.
- **Candia** is in the last year of its 21-year siege; Venice is desperate, and desperate states make mistakes.
- **The Solovetsky Monastery** refuses the new rite, and the tsar's siege begins.
- **Stenka Razin's Cossacks** are raiding the Caspian coast, Persia's included.
- **Poland's king,** John II Casimir, abdicates, and an election is coming (general knowledge, not in the research files).
- **The red alert.** A Viennese lady has a Mutapan lamp in her drawing room. The emperor's counsellors know what it means.

> **Further in:** in our history, Kara Mustafa reaches the walls of Vienna in 1683.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The pamphlets.** German pamphlets say Sweden wins its wars by Sámi sorcery, and the chancellor wants a scholar to prove otherwise (in our history, Schefferus's *Lapponia*, 1673). Here someone has to decide what's true, in a kingdom with a witch panic of its own.
- **The drum in the cabinet.** A seized Sámi drum sits in a prince's cabinet of curiosities, and its owner wants it back.
- **The Venice Job.** Something is going on the market soon and will command a hefty fee.
- **Blåkulla.** What carries the children off, if anything, is each table's to decide.
- **The Giant of the Black Forest,** a Ranger, and a clearing.
- **A benandante before the Inquisition** says he fought something on the Ember Days, and he has the wounds.
- **The Polish election.** Every court has a candidate, and some of the electors can be bought with magic.

data.name: The Ottomans and the Islamic West

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
In 1668 the Ottoman Empire matches or outstrips Europe. It holds three continents' worth of coast, besieges Venetian Crete, and already has what Europe is still arguing about: a chief astrologer at court, centuries of hospitals, and a learned magic in Arabic before Europe had it. Its quarrel isn't over who licenses magic but over what counts as piety.

**The one thing to remember:** the Islamic world isn't behind Europe in magic; it's older at it. The fight here is between the Sufi lodges and the preachers who call their practice illicit innovation, and in 1666 the preachers won a round.

> **Further in:** the Emerald Tablet, the Hermetic text Europe's wizards are named for, first appears in Arabic.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Not desert: cold Anatolian and Iranian plateaus with snowy winters, the Caspian's wet forest shore, the cedar and oak of the Atlas and Zagros, and Yemen's monsoon terraces.

- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age hit here too. Cold and drought in the 1590s broke the system that fed Istanbul and the army, fed the Celali revolts, and emptied Anatolian villages; the recovery is still incomplete.
- **The herders.** Turkmen and Yörük nomads move between winter lowlands and summer *yayla*; Bedouin graze the Syrian steppe.
- **The Nile.** Egypt lives on the summer flood, fed by Ethiopia's monsoon. A reading at the Rawda Nilometer sets the year's taxes; a low flood means famine.
- **Animals.** Lions in the Atlas, Mesopotamia and Iran; locust swarms that strip a district in hours.
- **Disease.** Plague is endemic, recurring every few years from the ports. Healing magic tempers every epidemic, but healers, druids and clerics are not common, so they blunt an outbreak and can't stop one.

> **Further in:** in 1668 lion cubs are still sent to rulers as diplomatic gifts in the Maghreb.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Porte.** Sultan Mehmed IV reigns; the Köprülü grand viziers run the state. Köprülü Mehmed exiled the militant preachers to Cyprus in 1656; his son Fazıl Ahmed is pressing the siege of Candia in person (general knowledge, not in the research files).
- **The janissaries** were once Christian-born boys levied from the Balkans; the levy has faded, but the corps can still make and unmake sultans, and killed Osman II in 1622.
- **The minister of magic** is the chief astrologer, the *müneccimbaşı*, who keeps the calendars and picks auspicious hours. In 1577 one of them, Taqi al-Din, built a Galata observatory as fine as Tycho's; it was demolished in 1580.
- **Egypt** has an Ottoman governor, but the beys rule: rival households of bought, trained and freed soldiers, split into the Faqāriyya and the Qāsimiyya.
- **The Regencies** of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli are Ottoman on paper, self-governing military states in fact. In Algiers the janissary agha seized power from the pasha in 1659, and the corsair captains' guild, the *taifa*, is a constitutional body; Tunis has a dey and a bey, and the bey is winning; Tripoli changes rulers by coup.
- **"The Regencies"** in the book's own prose (Scott, 2026-10-27). "Barbary" is Europe's name for the coast, from "Berber" by way of "barbarian"; it's their word, not the coast's.
- **Morocco** was never Ottoman. Mawlāy al-Rashīd of the ʿAlawī family took Fez in 1666 and is taking the rest. For decades the strongest state in the north was the Dilāʾ, a Sufi lodge with a library.
- **Safavid Persia**, the Ottomans' Shiʿi neighbor and at peace with them since 1639, has its own section (see Safavid Persia).
- **The conquered.** Balkan Christians gave sons to the levy; Crimean Tatar raids sold Polish and Russian captives at Caffa.

> **Further in:** the Topkapı Palace keeps a talismanic shirt that took three years to make, because each stage had to wait for the right star.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Scott's rule: the Islamic world's learned magic is Hermeticism too. Real Hermeticism was deeply shaped by Arabic scholarship, so the Children of the Emerald Tablet run from London to Constantinople from a shared root, but these schools are their own, not a reskin of the Western ones.

- **The science of letters** (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*) holds that the Arabic letters are tied to creation and works through their numerical values, the names of God, and magic squares. Its classic grimoire, the *Shams al-maʿārif* attributed to al-Būnī, took its best-known form in the 17th century: new around 1668. Jurists condemned the science as sorcery; elite Sufi and scholarly circles copied it widely.
- **Talismans.** Rulers commission shirts covered in Qurʾanic text, divine names, magic squares and astrological signs, worn under armor; ordinary people wear folded paper amulets from a *hoca* or *fqih* against the jinn and the evil eye.
- **Healing.** Qurʾanic recitation, amulets, and the *baraka* of saints' tombs, where the possessed are brought. With hospitals centuries old (al-Mansuri in Cairo, al-Nuri in Damascus, the *darüşşifa*s of Istanbul), the Islamic world wonders what the fuss about Lanternhall is.
- **Holy warriors and clerics.** Holiness works for anyone actually holy. On the Swahili coast and the Zambezi, Islam's holy warriors can actually do the holy work, one reason Mutapa stopped where it did.
- **The anti-magic faction.** The Kadızadeli preachers condemn shrine visits, saint veneration, Sufi music and dance, coffee, tobacco and Ibn ʿArabī's teachings as illicit innovation. In 1666 Mehmed IV banned the Mevlevi whirling ceremony and the Halveti *dhikr*. The whirling is a working, a remembrance that opens the dervish to God, so the ban took magic off Istanbul's streets as well as music. The lodges still turn, behind closed doors.

> *"They closed the lodge, so we turn in the cellar. The preacher says it's innovation. The sick man we turned for walked home."* (a Mevlevi dervish in Istanbul)

> **Further in:** the Qurʾan says Solomon commanded the jinn, who built for him. Europe's Solomonic conjurers take their name from the same king.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The beings closest to fair folk belong to living religion, recorded mostly in scripture or 19th- and 20th-century ethnography.

**Jinn are part of revealed religion, not folklore,** and calling them fairies or monsters can offend. **The jinn are what Islam says they are** (Scott): a moral people of smokeless fire, under God's judgment, and not part of the Hidden.

- **The jinn** marry, have children, die, and will be judged like humans; some are believers. They live in ruins, wells, bathhouses, drains and thresholds and punish harm done to them, even by accident, so people say *bismillāh* (in Turkish, *destur*, "by your leave") before pouring hot water. Iron repels them, as it does European fairies.
- **The edge doesn't fit.** Jinn live inside the threshold, not past the village edge, and the Bedouin and Yörük who move with their herds have no village edge at all.
- **The parī**, at home in Persia (see Safavid Persia), are the closest here to European fairies. Turkish peris fly in green cloud-garments.
- **The ghul** haunts the desert, takes any shape but can't change its ass's hooves, and calls travelers by name. One blow kills it; a second revives it.
- **The div**, from the *Shahnameh*, is ogre more than fairy, and hides its soul outside its body.
- **Childbed spirits.** The Āl, or *albastı*, attacks mothers and newborns; iron under the pillow guards against it (not checked in the research). It's the nearest parallel to Europe's fear of stolen children.
- **The taken and returned** is less often a fairy's captive than the *majdhūb*, "one drawn," seized by God and revered as a saint, or Khiḍr, the Green One, who meets travelers and vanishes.
- **Not yet here.** Zar possession is first recorded in 1839; in 1668 it would be two centuries early.
- **Hidden Killers** patrol rural villages here as everywhere. The Wild Hunt rides here too.

> **Further in:** in a 2012 survey, 86% of Moroccan Muslims said they believe in jinn. There, the healing brotherhood of the Hamadsha seeks out ʿAisha Qandisha, a spirit-woman with hooves who lives by the water. How early her cult is attested is unclear.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
The freeze-frame:

- **Candia.** The siege of Venetian Crete, begun in 1648, is in what in our history is its last year.
- **The Mevlevi ban** is two years old, and the preachers are pressing.
- **Sabbatai Zevi,** the claimed Jewish messiah, converted to Islam before the sultan in 1666.
- **Persia** crowns its shah a second time, at a better hour (see Safavid Persia).
- **Morocco.** Al-Rashīd annexes the Dilāʾ and moves about 1,300 Jewish families from there to Fez.
- **Evliya Çelebi** is on the road through Greece, Crimea and Rumelia, recording shrines.
- **Mutapa.** Its trade runs through Muslim hands, from the Swahili coast to Gujarat, and it doesn't want to antagonize the Islamic world. Constantinople still matters, but now there's Sofala. A customer and a careful partner: Mutapa sells into the Ottoman world through Muslim merchants, and the Porte would rather tax that trade than fight over it.

> **Further in:** the Porte has a chief astrologer and a court of Hermetic scholars.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Candia's endgame.** A Venetian commander, a grand vizier, and something in the citadel neither wants the other to have.
- **The cellar lodge.** A banned Mevlevi circle, a Kadızadeli informer, and a sick man who needs the turning.
- **The captives.** Algiers holds tens of thousands of captives, Malta and Livorno hold Muslim galley slaves, and a ransom broker works both sides.
- **A renegade captain** from Haarlem or Calabria, with a Mutapan device he took off a Portuguese prize.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
Safavid Persia is a large, settled empire at peace with all its neighbors, and in 1668 it is watching the sky. Isfahan is among the largest cities in the world, and its Armenian suburb runs a trading network from Amsterdam to Manila. After a year of famine and a great earthquake, the court decided the shah had been crowned at the wrong hour, and on Nowruz 1668 it crowned him again under a new name.

**The one thing to remember:** in Persia the people who read the stars hold real power, and the people who read the Law are rising to take it from them. The hour is a matter of state, and an hour can be chosen again.

> **Further in:** follow the silk. It leaves Gilan with New Julfa's Armenians for Venice and Amsterdam (see Central and Eastern Europe), crosses to Aleppo and Smyrna (see the Ottomans and the Islamic West), or goes down to Bandar Abbas and out onto the Monsoon Road (see the Indian Ocean). East, the road runs through Kandahar to the Mughals (see Mughal India); north, across the Caspian, Cossacks and Uzbeks (see the Steppe and the North).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
A high plateau ringed by mountains, with salt desert at its heart and every town placed where water can be brought to it.

- **The qanats.** Tunnels carry groundwater by gravity for kilometers out of the mountains to the oasis towns. A dead qanat is mourned, and the town ends where its water does.
- **The deserts.** The Dasht-e Kavir and the Lut are salt and stone, the caravans' country and the ghul's.
- **The Caspian shore.** Gilan and Mazandaran are wet, forested, rice and silk country, and crown land. Abbas I's palace town, **Farahabad**, is here.
- **Earthquakes.** In November 1667 one struck Shirvan and killed over 30,000 in its villages and about 20,000 in Shamakhi, the silk town.
- **Disease and hunger.** Drought, locusts and famine hit in 1666–67, with food riots. Healing and purifying magic soften a lean year, but its casters are few, so they can't stop one (Scott).

> *"The Franks ask how many guns the shah has. Ask how many astrolabes. He has more of those, and he uses them."* (a clerk of the royal workshops in Isfahan)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The shah.** Solayman, about 21, was crowned as Safi II in October 1666 and again in March 1668. Raised in the harem by eunuchs and Turkish-speaking at home, he drinks heavily, governs more and more from the harem, and will never lead an army.
- **The inner council.** His mother, a Circassian named Nakihat Khanom, and three senior eunuchs, Agha Kafur, Agha Mobarak and Agha Kamal, decide what reaches him; a secret council of eunuchs is reported to have sidelined the formal council of state.
- **The grand vizier.** Mirza Mohammad Karaki runs the administration outside the harem. In our history he falls in 1669 to Shaykh Ali Khan Zanganeh, a Kurdish noble.
- **The clergy.** Sabzavari, *shaykh al-islam* of Isfahan, presided over both coronations. Behind him, Majlesi, about 40, is compiling a vast hadith collection and putting doctrine into plain Persian. The clergy are a confident establishment now, beginning to push the shah.
- **The army.** The *qizilbash*, the Turkmen cavalry who won the dynasty its throne, are shrinking: their elite guard is down from 2,000 to 700. The **ghulams**, Georgian, Armenian and Circassian captives and converts, serve as cavalry, officials and governors.
- **Georgia.** Vakhtang V of Kartli converted in Isfahan as Shahnavaz Khan, "beloved of the shah," and was crowned at Mtskheta in the Orthodox rite: a governor to Isfahan, a Christian king at home. His son Archil rules Kakheti.
- **New Julfa.** About 30,000 Armenians, deported here in 1604–05, elect their own mayor, ship the empire's silk, and pay the queen mother's stipend in taxes. With her backing they have pushed the Catholic missionaries out of the suburb.
- **Bandar Abbas**, hot and feverish, holds Dutch and English factories that loathe each other; the Dutch have had the upper hand since 1645.
- **Kandahar** has been Persian since 1649; the Mughals' heaviest guns failed against it in 1653 and they gave up.
- **The conquered.** Jews were forcibly converted twice, most recently in 1656–62 (another account dates it 1645–54). Zoroastrians in Yazd and Kerman are squeezed for taxes and labor by officials of Isfahan and of the province alike.

> **Further in:** a Capuchin, Raphaël du Mans, has been the court's interpreter since about 1650. Every European who writes about Persia learns it from him.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Persia gives its court astrologers real power (Scott). Here the hour is a working, and the men who choose it sit near the throne.

- **The chief astrologer** casts the *ekhtiyarat*, the "elections": the propitious moment for an audience, a journey, a campaign, a building or a coronation, read mainly from the moon. He presents the year's almanac at Nowruz and stands near the shah with an astrolabe (details unverified). Nobody in the sources names who held the office in 1668.
-
- **The wrong hour.** When famine and the earthquake followed the first coronation, the physicians blamed the astrologers for the date, and the queen mother, the chief physician and the chief eunuchs ordered a second ceremony. One account has the astrologers joining the verdict.
- **The substitute king.** Tavernier tells of a Zoroastrian set on the throne first, then replaced by a statue that was beheaded, so the bad stars would fall elsewhere. Treat it as Tavernier's story.
- **The physicians against the astrologers.** Two learned professions, both with court offices, compete to explain every disaster.
- **Talismans.** Abbas I's chief astrologer, Molla Jalal, is credited with a treatise of talismans: one to "tie the tongue," one that shielded a minister from an audit, others for the women of the harem (the attribution is argued).
- **The clergy's days.** Theologians condemn astrology as denying God's power, and Shi'i scholars keep lists of lucky and unlucky days from the Imams' sayings; Majlesi is credited with one (unverified). The clergy's days against the astrologers' hours is the quarrel of the age.
- **The clergy against the Sufis.** The dynasty began as a Sufi order, and the shah is still nominally its "perfect guide," but the order is ceremonial now and the polemics against Sufis are multiplying. Sufi remembrance is a real working, as in Istanbul's lodges, so the campaign takes magic off Isfahan's streets as well as music.
- **The philosophers** of the School of Isfahan still teach, but Abbas II protected them, and he is dead.
- **Holiness works for anyone actually holy:** a Shi'i jurist, an Armenian priest, a Zoroastrian priest at Yazd's fire, a rabbi in Kashan.

**At the table.**

-
-

> **Further in:** in our history an astrologer's warning kept Solayman inside his palace for years before he died in 1694, and in 1722 the last Safavid shah delayed battle on his astrologers' advice, fed his troops a broth to make them invisible, and lost Isfahan.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
**A note on the name.** In Twelver Shi'ism the Twelfth Imam is called the Hidden Imam, in occultation since 874. He has nothing to do with the setting's Hidden: he is a holy figure of a living faith, and nothing in Euphonia makes him fae. This chapter calls the fae by their own name, the pari.

- **The jinn** are what Islam says they are (Scott): a moral people of smokeless fire, under God's judgment, and not fae. Persian translators rendered *jinn* as *div* or *pari*, and the learned count the pari among the jinn. By Scott's test, the pari are fae that took the jinn's name.
- **The pari.** This is their homeland. Once Avestan demonesses, they are now supremely beautiful and morally mixed. They carry people off to **Paristan**, sometimes to a pari wedding, in body or in trance, and make love matches with humans that end when a taboo is broken. They are one people from Isfahan to Delhi to the Kazakh steppe (see Mughal India and the Steppe and the North), and Paristan is the Persianate name for their realm. People avoid naming them and say *az ma behtaran*, "those better than us" (general knowledge).
- **The Āl** is the childbed spirit of Iran, Armenia and the Caucasus: a thin old woman with a clay nose who carries off a new mother's liver; if she reaches water with it, the mother dies. In Armenian lore she steals a baby within forty days of birth and leaves an imp in its place. Iron, onions, garlic and prayer guard the forty days. The tradition calls her a demon. Her Persian record before the 19th century wasn't checked (unverified).
- **The ghul-e biyaban** haunts the caravan roads between the oases, calling travelers by name.
- **The qanats** are male and female, and in the Kashan region they are married to keep the water flowing (recorded in 2014, age unknown).
- **Not the pari:** the jinn; the Twelve Imams; Khidr, the Green One; the Zoroastrian yazatas and Ahriman; the fravashis; the divs, demons like the *Shahnameh*'s White Div (though a table may treat a folk tale's div as a pari in an ogre's shape); and the **Simurgh**, nearer the divine than the fae.
- **The edge** fits the oasis towns: past the last garden is the waste. The Zagros herders, who move between summer and winter pastures, have none.
- **The raiding season.** The Wild Hunt rides through the northern dark half, Samhain to Beltane.

> **Further in:** the pari of the *Shahnameh* are persecuted and caged by divs. Nobody has asked the pari who holds the keys now.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The second coronation.** On Nowruz, 20 March (one source says the 24th), at nine in the morning, in the Chehel Sotun, Safi II is crowned again as **Solayman**. A comet follows; the sources disagree whether the astrologers read it as a portent or a good omen.
- **Razin on the Caspian.** Stenka Razin's Cossacks fail at Derbent, raid toward Baku, lose about 400 men at Rasht, and send envoys to Isfahan asking for land (whether Razin himself went is (unverified)). Then they pose as merchants in **Farahabad** and sack it.
- **Basra.** The Ottomans take Basra, on the Gulf border, back into direct rule. Peace has held with them since 1639.
- **The jewelers.** Tavernier sells Louis XIV a 116-carat blue diamond. Chardin, Abbas II's jewel buyer, saw both coronations and will publish them in Paris in 1671.
- **The rising cleric.** Majlesi is compiling the *Oceans of Lights* and writing for ordinary readers. In our history he girds the next shah himself in 1694, in place of the Sufi who always had.
- **The Book of the Forced Converts.** In Kashan, Babai ben Lotf is setting down the history of his community's forced conversions in Persian verse in Hebrew letters, including the day Fayz Kashani interceded for them. Most converts have probably returned to Judaism (unverified).

> **Further in:** in our history Razin's Cossacks destroy a Persian fleet off Pig Island in July 1669. The legend that he drowned a Persian princess in the Volga comes from a Dutch sailor, and historians doubt it.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The wrong hour.** One side at court needs the new hour to hold; another needs it to fail. The party is hired to check a rival's chart.
- **The substitute.** A man who sat on the throne for a few minutes is walking around Isfahan with a shah's bad stars.
- **The eunuchs' gate.** A petition, a warning or a Mutapan gift has to reach the shah, and it has to get past Agha Kafur, Agha Mobarak and Agha Kamal first.
- **The merchants at Farahabad.** The Cossacks have been buying for a week, and the party is in town when they stop.
- **Kerman's tax.** Isfahan's collectors and the province's both claim the same Zoroastrian community, and its own collector is caught between. No villain here is simply religious.
- **The forty days.** A Georgian ghulam's wife has given birth. The midwives have their iron and onions, but something has already carried her liver toward the river, and the child in the cradle may not be hers.
- **The pari wedding.** A New Julfa merchant's son went to one at Nowruz and hasn't come back, and his family's letters reach from Amsterdam to Manila.
- **Bandar Abbas in fever season.** Someone has brought a Mutapan lamp ashore, and the shah's astrologers want to know what star it answers to.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
West Africa in 1668 is a crowded field of strong states: Muslim cavalry kingdoms in the Sahel, the Yoruba kingdoms and their holy city, gold states in the Akan forest, a sacred king at Benin, and slave-trading kingdoms on the lagoons.

**The one thing to remember:** the Europeans are tenants. Every fort stands on ground an African ruler rents out, and what the coast sells, and to whom, is decided ashore. In 1668 it sells gold, and more and more it sells people.

> **Further in:** the caravans go north to Morocco (the Ottomans and the Islamic West); the ships go west to Brazil and Barbados (South America), north to Amsterdam and London (Western Europe), or south to Luanda (West-Central Africa).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
The bands run east to west: desert edge, savanna, forest, coast.

- **The Sahel and the savanna.** Camel country on the Sahara's edge, with the desert ports (Timbuktu, Gao, Agadez); south of it, millet, cattle and horses, the country of the cavalry states.
- **The forest.** Farmed, tapped and full of towns and shrines: Benin, Ijebu, Ilesa and the Akan kingdoms are forest states. The **Dahomey Gap**, where savanna reaches the sea west of Allada, is the one road a horse can take to the coast.
- **The tsetse line.** The fly kills horses, so cavalry can raid the forest but can't live in it. Oyo can't breed enough horses of its own and buys them from Nupe and Borgu, the neighbors it fights.
- **The coast.** Lagoons and mangrove creeks east of the Volta; surf on the gold shore, where canoemen ferry every cargo out to the ships.
- **The harmattan**, the dusty wind off the Sahara, blows roughly November to March: the caravan and campaign season.
- **Fever.** Malaria and yellow fever kill newcomers on the coast at very high rates (unverified: no figures for the 1660s); healers are too few to stop it (Scott). No European army operates inland anywhere here.
- **The names.** Europeans call the shores the Gold Coast and the Slave Coast: the cargo, not the people.

> *"The Dutchman asks where the gold comes from. I tell him: from upriver. He builds a fort upriver. We burn it. Then he asks again."* (an Akan broker at Elmina)

> **Further in:** from 1668 the English Mint strikes West African gold into a coin with an elephant on it, named for the coast: the guinea.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
**The Yoruba world.** A family of kingdoms with one language, one holy city and one sacred line of kings, not one empire.

- **Ile-Ife** is the homeland: its king, the **Ooni**, descends from Oduduwa, as all the crowned Yoruba kings claim to. Its weight is sacred, not military.
- **Oyo** is the rising power, home from decades of exile after the Nupe took its capital. Abipa brought the court back around 1610, and tradition calls him "the king who caught ghosts," for the nobles who dressed as phantoms to scare him off.
- **The Alaafin isn't absolute.** The seven councillors of the **Oyo Mesi**, led by the **Basorun**, choose him and can order him to take his own life; the crown prince must die with his father. The alaafin in 1668 was probably **Ajagbo** (unverified).
- **The Ogboni**, the society of elders tied to the Earth, judge bloodshed and mediate between council and king.
- **The others** (Ijebu, Ilesa, Owo, Ketu, the Egba towns) are independent and often hostile; Ilesa's forest fought Oyo's cavalry to a standstill.
- **Oyo and the trade.** Oyo forbids enslaving its own subjects and in 1668 taxes the trade more than it feeds it. In our history that changes in the next century.

**The lagoon kingdoms.**

- **Allada** controls the ports of Offra and Whydah and is the great slave-selling kingdom of its coast: about 125,000 people between 1640 and 1690. It pays tribute to Oyo. Its king is probably **Tezifon** (unverified).
- **Dahomey** is a small inland kingdom on the Abomey plateau under its first king, Houegbadja.

**The forest kings.**

- **Benin's oba** no longer leads armies: he is a sacred king secluded in a palace hung with brass plaques, and his chiefs are taking the power he doesn't use. Who reigns in the 1660s is uncertain (unverified).
- **Warri**, in the Delta, is a Christian kingdom whose late king studied at Coimbra.
- **Denkyira** is the great Akan power under **Boa Amponsem I**, with a treasury called the *Sikadan*, "house of gold." The future Asante are among its tributaries.
- **Akwamu**, behind Accra, is a rising military state with musketeers and hereditary slave-soldiers, eyeing Great Accra.
- **The coastal kingdoms** (Fetu, Eguafo, the Fante towns) host the forts and play the companies off against each other.

**The savanna and the Sahel.**

- **Bornu**'s **Mai Ali** has been to Mecca three times, the last in 1667, and came home to a revolt.
- **Kano and Katsina**, the leading Hausa cities, made peace to face the **Kwararafa**, the "salt people" of the Benue, who broke into Kano in 1653.
- **The Arma**, heirs of the Moroccan army that broke Songhay in 1591, rule Timbuktu and the Niger bend from river forts and stopped answering to Morocco in 1660. Their pashas rarely last a year.
- **The Mossi** kings are horse lords who stayed out of Islam; earth priests of the older people keep their offices beside them.

**Senegambia.**

- **The Wolof** kingdoms (Cayor, Waalo, Jolof) are ruled by warrior aristocracies, the *ceddo*, who fund their armies by selling captives.
- **Kaabu**, a Mandinka federation, grows rich on war captives; no European has ever reached its walled capital at Kansala.
- **The Futas.** Futa Toro has a Denianke king and a community of Muslim scholars; Futa Jallon is a highland of Fulbe herders and farmers.

**The tenants.**

- **The Dutch West India Company** is strongest, from **Elmina**, taken from Portugal in 1637.
- **The English** Royal Adventurers hold **Cape Coast Castle** and **James Island** in the Gambia. Their 1663 charter names the slave trade, and their captives are branded "DoY," for the Duke of York.
- **The Danes** hold **Christiansborg**, bought from Great Accra's king; **the French** have Saint-Louis on the Senegal. The Swedes gave up at Breda last year.

> **Further in:** in 1665 the Dutch stormed the English fort at Kormantin with about 1,200 African allies, while Jan Kabessa's men fought for the English. African armies decide which company keeps its forts.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Every tradition here is a Wisdom tradition or a learned one, and most are both.

- **The Yoruba are West Africa's Andes** (Scott): the Indigenous power whose Wisdom tradition makes it a match for anyone. It belongs to the Yoruba as a people, not to one kingdom: Ifá's priests serve them all. In the field it looks like **spirit riding**, the orisha mounting their devotees, along with other divine interventions (Scott). Whether that power gathers at Ife, the holy city, at Oyo, the empire, or at both is each table's to decide (Scott).
- **Ifá** is learned Wisdom. A *babaláwo*, "father of secrets," casts palm nuts or a divination chain to find one of 256 *odu*, chants its verses and prescribes sacrifice. It reads signs rather than using possession, and kings consult it before every great decision.
- **The orisha** answer their priests: holiness works for anyone actually holy. Shango, remembered as a king of Oyo, is thunder; lightning-struck stones are kept at his shrines. Ogun clears roads and works iron. Eshu carries offerings between the worlds and is not the Devil, whatever later missionaries made of him.
- **The Ogboni's brass staffs**, cast in pairs and joined by a chain, are held to be the Earth's vessel, not its picture.
- **Benin's oba** has his mystical power renewed each year in the Igue rite; the *obo*, diviner-herbalists, cure, counter witches and administer ordeals.
- **The Akan *okomfo*** is a priest-medium possessed by a god after years of training; *asuman* are charms a god can live in.
- **Vodun.** Allada and Whydah have their own gods; Whydah keeps a royal python. The later, well-known Dahomean pantheon was built after 1668.
- **Islam's learning.** Timbuktu's family libraries survived conquest; Katsina's scholars are known for mathematics and the occult sciences, the science of letters and sand-divination among them. Islam's holy warriors can actually do the holy work here, as on the Swahili coast.
- **The secret societies.** Poro and Sande, in the Sierra Leone forests, take the young into seclusion and return them initiated; they can overrule chiefs. What outsiders know is what members chose to show.
- **The fever.**

> **Further in:** Ifá's binary signs closely resemble Arabic sand-divination, *khatt al-raml*; scholars disagree on how the two are related (unverified). The Saharan books come south from the same world as the Ottomans' science of letters.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Nearly all of this is 19th- and 20th-century record of living belief; the 17th-century record is European traders calling everything "fetish."

- **The bori spirits** (Hausa). Spirits of families, places, animals and rocks, sorted into twelve "houses" and handled by the *bori* possession cult, mostly women, led in some kingdoms by a chief priestess, the **Inna**. Muslim Hausa call them *aljannu*, jinn. They aren't jinn: they're Hidden that took the jinn's name (Scott).
- **The aziza** (Fon). Little people of anthills and silk-cotton trees who give hunters good magic and are said to have taught people fire. The winged aziza of later fantasy rests on one late source.
- **The mmoatia** (Akan). Forest little people about a foot high, with backward feet and whistling speech, who teach herbal medicine to priests (unverified). Sasabonsam, who hooks travelers from the trees, is more ogre than fae.
- **The egbere** (Yoruba). Short, weeping night-walkers of the woods; whoever takes an egbere's little mat grows rich.
- **The iroko's spirit** (Yoruba). Whoever sees the Iroko-man face to face goes mad and soon dies, and a felled iroko must be prayed over.
- **The water.** Benin's Olokun and the Yoruba river orisha are gods, not Hidden. Water spirits of wealth and seduction are old here; the name Mami Wata isn't recorded until 1775.
- **The owners of the land.** Every forest, river and rock has owners, and an earth priest bargains with them: the Mossi *tengasoba*, the Yoruba and Edo groves, the Poro forest. This is the region's village edge, and the Hidden Killers watch it. The Wild Hunt rides here too.

> **Further in:** the aziza, the mmoatia and the egbere all give something a person can use: luck, medicine, wealth. Here the Hidden teach professions.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
The freeze-frame:

- **The trade is growing.** Nearly half a million people were shipped from all of Africa in 1651–75, and the number is rising. A Dutch report puts Offra alone at 2,500–3,000 a year around 1670 (unverified: weak citation); the desert trade still takes about 7,000 a year north.
- **Who sells:** Allada's king through his ports, the Wolof *ceddo* and Kaabu's warlords from their wars, coastal brokers between the companies. **Who resists:** Muslim scholars who refuse to sell Muslims to Christians, Benin, which restricts the sale of men (unverified), and the people who run.
- **The English** Royal Adventurers are in debt from the war, and turning to captives.
- **Dapper's book**, out in Amsterdam this year, describes Benin's brass palace to Europe.
- **Oyo** holds its northern line against Nupe and Borgu and looks southwest, toward Egbado and Allada.
- **Bornu.** Mai Ali, home from Mecca, is putting down a revolt.
- **Timbuktu** has been its own master for eight years, and Morocco has a strong new sultan (the Ottomans and the Islamic West).

> **Further in:** in South America, Spain's mines in the Chocó run on enslaved Africans, and Palmares is a free kingdom of escaped ones. Mutapa is African, and rising.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The salt people.** In our history the Kwararafa break Kano again in 1671, and a Katsina scholar's prayers are credited with killing their commander.
- **The penitents.** A Saharan preacher north of the Senegal calls for repentance and an end to slave raiding; in our history his movement topples four kingdoms in 1673 and shuts down the French trade for a season.
- **Akwamu and Great Accra.** A rising army, a rich neighbor, and a Danish castle whose landlord may change.
- **Morocco's new sultan will want Timbuktu back,** and the Arma don't agree on whether to say yes.
- **The tsetse line.** A druid or a healer who can keep a horse alive in the forest moves Oyo's frontier, and every kingdom south of it knows that.
- **The mat.** A trader at Ijebu market is suddenly, inexplicably rich.
- **The roads at Offra.** A company ship loading captives, and a family ashore come to buy one of them back.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
West-Central Africa is a Christian kingdom with its crown in pieces. Kongo has been Catholic for 150 years, with its own nobles, schools and books in Kikongo, and in 1665, at Mbwila, an army from Portuguese Luanda killed its king and much of its nobility. Two royal houses now fight over the throne. The power rising out of the wreck is **Soyo**, Kongo's own coastal province at the mouth of the Congo, rich on salt and Dutch trade, which has beaten every army sent against it (Scott).

**The one thing to remember:** the question in 1668 is whether Soyo reunites Kongo before Portugal, Matamba or the civil war decides it (Scott). Soyo's counts have always found a weak king more useful than a strong one. Rising and reuniting aren't the same thing, and Soyo hasn't decided which it wants.

> **Further in:** this is the busiest slaving coast in the Atlantic, and nearly everyone here is part of it, Soyo included. Its ships go to Brazil (see South America), its governors come from there, and its trophies go to Lisbon (see Western Europe). North up the coast lies the West Africa chapter; around the Cape, Mutapa and the Indian Ocean.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The river that swallows rivers.** The Congo (*Nzadi*) pours out more water than any river but the Amazon. Soyo holds its south bank and the old port of Mpinda.
- **The falls.** Above the estuary the river drops through some 32 falls and rapids over about 350 km. No ship passes; everything beyond, from the Tio markets at Malebo Pool inward, is reached on foot or by canoe.
- **The Kwanza** is Portugal's road inland, a corridor of river forts; **the Kwango** to the east is the edge of the Atlantic's reach, where Kasanje holds the farthest market.
- **The country.** Savanna and wooded hills, dense forest along the rivers and in the Mayombe north of the Congo; drier toward the Namib in the south. One long rainy season, roughly October to May, and a cool dry season, the *cacimbo* (unverified).
- **The fever coast.** Newcomers from Europe die at catastrophic rates, and horses rarely survive (cause unverified). Portugal's armies here are mostly African, led by a few hundred musketeers, many of them convicts sent from Brazil. Healers temper the epidemics, smallpox above all, but are too few to stop them.
- **Money is cloth and shells.** Raffia squares are currency from Loango to Luanda; *nzimbu* shells from Luanda island were the Kongo king's money until Portugal took the island around 1650.

> *"In São Salvador they pay the teacher in shells. In Luanda they pay the soldier in cloth. Nobody pays anyone in Portuguese coin, including the Portuguese."* (a Vili trader at Mpinda)

> **Further in:** Diogo Cão's men cut their king's name into the cliffs above the Yellala falls in 1482. They couldn't get past them either.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The king at São Salvador.** Álvaro VIII, of the Kinlaza house, holds the capital because Soyo put him there in 1666. He has ceded mining rights in Mbamba and Mpemba to Portugal (1667), which his nobles haven't forgiven.
- **The houses.** The **Kinlaza** and the **Kimpanzu** (*kanda*, royal lineages) each claim the throne. A Kimpanzu rival, Afonso II, holds out at Nkondo in the east; a Kinlaza rival, Pedro III, is already counting Álvaro's guards.
- **The electors.** Kongo's king is chosen by senior officeholders, and one of them is the ruler of Soyo. The European titles (duke, marquis, count) were put on Kongo offices in the 1500s; they stand for the rank, not the rank itself.
- **Soyo.** Count **Paulo da Silva** rules the richest province in Kongo: the only one with a port and salt, a capital of about 30,000, and a fortified sacred wood, **Nfinda Ngula**, that no army has taken. Soyo threw back four royal invasions (1641–1656), captured a king's son, and sent its own ambassador to Dutch Brazil. Its rulers call themselves princes now.
- **The Dutch** trade at Mpinda and sell Soyo guns and powder. They build no forts here; they anchor and deal.
- **Portuguese Angola.** Luanda, Benguela and a string of river forts reaching about 300 km inland. It has no governor: a junta has run it since February 1667. Its money, ships and last governors came from Brazil.
- **Matamba.** Queen Njinga died in 1663 and her sister Barbara in 1666. Barbara's husband, Njinga a Mona, an Imbangala-trained commander Njinga distrusted, has seized power; João Guterres, the man the Church wouldn't let Barbara marry, wants it.
- **Kasanje.** A war-state on the Kwango founded by Imbangala, a society built by initiation instead of kinship. Its king, **Pascoal**, strangled his adoptive father to take the throne and was baptized by a Capuchin two years later. He sells captives to Luanda as its "general."
- **Loango**, north of the river: a king baptized as Afonso in 1663, a Christian faction beaten in 1665, and **Vili** merchants carrying copper and cloth from the coast to Malebo Pool.
- **The conquered.** Every power here takes captives and sells them, Kongo's houses and Soyo as much as Luanda; the civil war has made the trade bigger and Soyo richer.

> **Further in:** Soyo has backed both houses at different times. It looks less like a partisan than a broker that backs whoever keeps the throne weak.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Kongo's church named its priests with the word for its healers. When the Jesuits and Kongolese teachers put the faith into Kikongo, "holy" became *nkisi*, the word for a spirit-charged object; a priest became an *nganga*; a church became *nzo a ukisi*, the house of holiness. In Euphonia, holiness works for anyone actually holy, whatever their church, and Kongo is the place that already said so in its own vocabulary.

- **The church is Kongolese.** It runs on noble lay teachers, the *mestres*, paid by the state in shells; on brotherhoods; on Kongo's own Order of Christ; and on a Jesuit college in São Salvador that taught the elite to read Latin. Since 1624 the bishop has lived in Luanda and ordains no Kongolese, so a village's holy work is done by whoever is holy.
- **The nganga** heals, divines, guards the community against the witch, and makes *minkisi* (sing. *nkisi*): pots, horns, shells and bundles holding spirit-charged substances, where the word names both the object and the spirit inside. In setting terms this is a Wisdom craft that houses a spirit.
- **The quarrel is with the Capuchins.** The Italian friars condemn the old practice as witchcraft piece by piece and burn minkisi when they can. Kongo's nobles keep both. The Capuchins' charms and the nganga's both work; that's the problem.
- **The cross was here first.** Kongo's brass crucifixes merge the Roman cross with Kongo's own X-shaped sign of the crossing between the living and the dead; one in the Met is also a funerary bundle. Brass Saint Anthony figures protect mothers and children.
- **Oath-takers and hunters.** Some minkisi seal treaties; the *nkondi* hunt wrongdoers. They're real in 1668, but the bristling nailed figures in museums are a 19th-century form. Here an nganga bangs minkisi together to wake them.
- **The witch.** *Kindoki* is the power to harm through the dead. Used in secret by one person, it's witchcraft; the *ndoki* is the community's enemy and the nganga its defense.
- **The Imbangala** keep the *ijila*, a law of the war camp, and anoint themselves with ***maji a samba***, an ointment said to make a warrior invulnerable while he keeps the law. The accounts come from outsiders with reasons to make them monstrous.
- **The book of the year.** Dapper's *Description of Africa*, published in Amsterdam in 1668, describes Loango's minkisi as both thing and spirit. Every minister of magic in Europe is reading it.

> *"The friar says my nkisi is the devil's. Then he blesses water and hangs it on the door. I ask him what the difference is, and he gets angry."* (an nganga near Mbanza Soyo)

> **Further in:** in our history, in 1704, a young nganga from near Kibangu, Kimpa Vita, will say Saint Anthony speaks through her and that Jesus was born in São Salvador.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Most of the detailed Kongo cosmology (the *kalunga* line, the *dikenga* cosmogram, the full roster of spirits) comes from 19th- and 20th-century ethnography and has to be read backward into 1668; the 17th-century record was written mostly by hostile friars and Dutch traders. These are living traditions, in Central Africa and across the Atlantic in Palo, Candomblé Angola and Vodou.

- **The bisimbi** (sing. *simbi*) are the region's Hidden: guardians of pools, streams, rocks and forests, called "minkisi of the water," who can appear as a person, a snake, a pot, a calabash vine or a spark of fire. Every pool has one, and a village asks before it draws.
- **Kianda**, the Mbundu spirit of the sea and protector of Luanda's fishermen, takes offerings thrown into the waves. Luanda's harbor is hers, whatever the junta thinks.
- **The dead are separate.** They live across the water in a mirror world where their night is our day (later sources). Ancestors (*bakulu*) are honored and fed; they are not the Hidden, and they don't ride with the Hunt.
- **The landholder.** The Mwene Kabunga kept a shrine near the capital and ritually challenged Kongo's conquest every year; the kings married into his line to share its authority. Whatever the first owners of the land bargained with is still owed.
- **The edge.** Soyo and Luanda keep the southern hemisphere's calendar, so the Wild Hunt rides through the southern winter, the dry season, milder near the equator.

> **Further in:** Soyo's sacred wood has turned back four kings. Nobody in Soyo says it was the muskets alone.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Soyo's king holds São Salvador,** barely. Álvaro VIII owes everything to Count Paulo and has paid for it in mines he gave Portugal.
- **Angola has no governor.** The junta waits for Lisbon; the soldiers wait for pay in cloth.
- **Matamba's throne** is held by a usurper and contested by a rival, and its council of nobles hasn't spoken.
- **The head in the chapel.** António I's head is buried in the chapel of Our Lady of Nazareth on Luanda's bay; Kongo's crown and sceptre are in Lisbon.
- **The northern trade.** Vili caravans carry copper from Mindouli and cloth to Malebo Pool, and the Dutch are about to start buying captives at Loango.
- **The Pungo a Ndongo rock.** Portugal's puppet king of Ndongo sits on his fortress with no army of his own, and his son is watching for Portugal to stumble.

> **Further in:** Mbwila's captives, nobles among them, went to Brazil. Some may be in Pernambuco now, near the hills where Palmares calls itself "Little Angola." (The story that a Kongo princess at Mbwila was Zumbi's grandmother doesn't fit the dates.)

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Kitombo is coming.** In our history, in January 1669 Pedro III kills Álvaro VIII; a new Kinlaza king calls in Portugal against Soyo, promising a fort to keep the Dutch out; and on 18 October 1670, at Kitombo, Soyo opens fire with Dutch cannon from its sacred wood and destroys the Portuguese army. Whether that happens here, and when, is the table's.
- **What Soyo wants.** A Soyo that crowns itself, a Soyo that reunites Kongo, and a Soyo that keeps Kongo broken and stays free are three different futures, and its counts turn over fast. Which one happens is your table's to decide (Scott).
- **The crown in Lisbon.** Whoever brings Kongo's regalia home has a claim no house can ignore (see Western Europe).
- **The rock.** Ndongo's heir is looking for allies, Matamba among them, to cut the road to Kasanje.
- **A pool that won't give water,** in a village that sold its simbi's neighbors downriver.
- **The Mutapan question.** An African power across the continent beats Europe with better-made magic. Soyo's envoys have been to Dutch Brazil; would they go to Sofala?

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
The Horn and the middle Nile are a crowd of powers, none of them a backwater. In the highlands a Christian emperor who claims descent from Solomon has just taken the throne at Gondar, a capital barely thirty years old. Around him are the Oromo, who rotate power by law every eight years; the walled Muslim city of Harar; an Ottoman coast; Yemen across the Red Sea, rich on coffee; and down the Blue Nile, the Funj sultans of Sennar at their height.

**The one thing to remember:** the empire threw out the Pope's men a generation ago, and Europe has called it closed ever since. It isn't: its envoys go to Yemen and to Aurangzeb, its sons command fleets in India, and in 1668 it is busy arguing with itself about who belongs inside the wall.

> **Further in:** follow the coffee. It leaves Mocha for Surat (see the Mughal India section), and the Gujarati brokers who finance it work the whole Monsoon Road (see the Indian Ocean section). Down the Red Sea, the pilgrims cross to Jeddah and the caravans go north to Egypt (see the Ottomans and the Islamic West).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
