A high plateau cut by gorges, falling away on every side to hot lowlands.

- **Height is everything.** Highlanders sort their land by altitude: hot *qolla* below, temperate *woina dega* in the middle, cool *dega* above about 2,600 m. The line down to the qolla is as much cultural as climatic.
- **The amba.** Flat-topped mountains with sheer sides serve as fortresses and royal prisons. On **Wehni**, the prison mountain, the new emperor's brothers wait out his reign.
- **The Blue Nile** runs out of Lake Tana, past island monasteries and royal tombs, then down a deep gorge to the Sudanese plain. It supplies almost 70 percent of the Nile's floodwater, and Egypt knows it. Ethiopian rulers were long credited with the power to turn the river aside and starve Egypt (unverified as a 17th-century claim; a well-known medieval motif).
- **The rains decide the war.** *Kiremt*, the great rains, run June to September and stop campaigning; armies march in the dry season after.
- **Coffee** grows wild in the southwest's forests and is first farmed around Harar; it reaches the world through Yemen.
- **Fever lives low.** Malaria haunts the valleys and lowlands, and the cool heights are largely free of it, one reason the highland states keep to the heights (general knowledge, not checked).

> *"The Franks say we shut the door. We shut it on the Franks. The Yemeni envoy found it open, and so did the Armenians."* (a court scribe at Gondar)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Power here is plural, and every state has its conquered peoples.

- **Yohannes I**, about 28, took the throne in October 1667; a council chose him and sent his brothers to Wehni. From his father's castles at **Gondar** he rules the northwest well, Tigray loosely, and the old heartland of Shewa hardly at all.
- **The Church.** The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the empire's great landlords. Its single bishop, the **Abuna**, is always an Egyptian monk sent from Alexandria, and he can undo even an emperor's marriage. In 1668 he was probably Marqos or Krestodolu (unverified; the list for these decades is unreliable). The monasteries hold the real weight, and they are at war over doctrine.
- **The Oromo** spent a century moving north and now hold much of the empire's old south and center. They rule themselves by **gadaa**: five classes take power in fixed order, and each ruling class serves eight years under an elected *abbaa gadaa*. If he dies in office, his widow holds the sceptre and proclaims the laws. Many serve in the emperor's armies.
- **The Beta Israel**, Ethiopia's Jews, lost their mountain kingdom in the 1620s. Landless now, they are the empire's masons, smiths and weavers, and Gondar's castles were raised largely by their hands (widely stated; not confirmed in the sources checked).
- **Harar**, a walled Muslim city-state, has been independent since 1647. **Emir Hashim ibn Ali** rules it, hemmed in by Oromo, Afar and Somali neighbors he handles by marriage and gifts more than by force.
- **The Ottomans** hold the coast on paper as the province of Habesh. Only Massawa has a governor; on the mainland opposite, the local *naib* holds the real power (unverified in detail).
- **Yemen.** The Zaydi imam **al-Mutawakkil Ismaʿil** drove the Ottomans out in the 1630s and grows rich on coffee shipped through Mocha, where English, French and Dutch factories sit beside Gujarati brokers.
- **Sennar.** The Funj sultan **Badi II** rules the Blue Nile below the escarpment from a fixed capital, on gold, caravan customs and a slave army taken in yearly raids on the Nuba Mountains. Funj noblewomen choose each sultan from his predecessors' sons, and a deposed sultan is executed by his own maternal uncle.
- **Darfur**, to the west, is a rising Fur sultanate sending slaves north on the forty days' road; its founding dates are disputed by decades.

> **Further in:** Ethiopia and Sennar have kept the peace since 1619. When Ethiopia wants rid of someone, Sennar is where it sends them.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Every faith here works, because holiness works for anyone actually holy. The quarrel isn't whether magic is real; it's who may touch it.

- **The tabot.** Every Orthodox church is consecrated by its *tabot*, a copy of the tablets of the Law; at Timkat the tabots go out through the streets.
- **The däbtära** are the region's learned magicians: unordained church scholars, cantors and poets, trained for decades in Ge'ez, chant and *qene*, the poetry of double meaning. They write God's secret names (*asmat*) on the skin of an animal killed in the patient's place, the client's name in red, and cut the scroll to the client's height. The church tolerates it: the texts are Christian.
- **The Net of Solomon,** an eight-pointed star, traps demons in its lines; on the scrolls St. Susenyos rides down Werzelya, who kills children. The demons are real, diabolical, and the saints fight them.
- **Reason.** At Enfraz, by Lake Tana, an old scholar named Zara Yaqob is finishing a book that tests every religion by reason. A Natural Philosopher would recognize the method at once.
- **Baraka.** Harar's shrines and the Funj holy men carry the blessing of the saints: in touch, tomb and curse. The *Tabaqat*'s wonders and curses are, here, what happened.
- **The qallu.** Among the Oromo, the *qallu* is possessed by the *ayyaana*, the spirits that carry the sky-god Waaqa's care to every living thing, and blesses the people in Waaqa's name.

> **Further in:** scholars have fought over the Hatata's authorship since 1920. The case now runs strongly for an Ethiopian author; whether it was this man is still open, and a party at Enfraz could find out.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The highlands' demons belong to the church and its saints, and the lowlands' jinn are what Islam says they are; neither is the Hidden. The Hidden here are quieter, and the record is late.

- **The hidden children.** A story tells how Eve hid some of her children from God, who decreed that the hidden ones stay hidden forever. In Euphonia they are the Hidden: humanity's own siblings, living beside it, possessing some, placated with hospitality rather than driven out. The story is recorded only in 20th-century ethnography (unverified for any earlier date), and zar ceremonies are first described in 1839, so none belongs in 1668 Gondar as fact.
- **The jinn's name.** In Muslim zar the hidden children later share ground with the jinn: by Scott's test, Hidden that took the jinn's name.
- **The trees.** Power lives in particular trees: the Amhara *adbar*, a community's guardian spirit, often housed in a great tree; the Qemant's cloth-wrapped *k'ole* and sacred groves. These are where the Hidden would hold their courts.
- **Not the Hidden:** the *ayyaana*, guardian spirits closer to angels than to the fae; and the gadaa assembly under its sycamore, which is a government, not a fae court.
- **No village edge.** For Afar, Somali and Oromo herders the edge is the waterless country between wells.
- **The raiding season.** North of the equator the Wild Hunt rides from Samhain to Beltane, through the dry season after the rains, the same months the armies march. Hidden Killers keep the villages here too.

> **Further in:** the hidden children are the nearest thing on the Monsoon Road to the Malay *orang bunian*, "the hidden people" (see the Indian Ocean section). Nobody on either shore has compared notes.

**Buda is not the Hidden, and not real.** Highlanders accuse artisans, above all smiths and the Beta Israel, of *buda*: the evil eye, and the power to become a hyena by night. In Euphonia the accusation is false, a prejudice the game shows and a party can expose, never a monster to hunt. The sources attest it only from the 19th century (unverified before then), though the stigma on artisans is older.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The council.** In his first year Yohannes calls a church council that rules on marriage between relatives and segregates Muslims, "Turks" and the Beta Israel. Gondar's Muslims get their own quarter at **Addis Alem**: segregation from one side, a recognized quarter from the other. Foreigners who refuse baptism into the Ethiopian church will be marched to Sennar next year.
- **The Hatata.** At Enfraz, Zara Yaqob, about 68, completes his *Hatata* (in 1667 or 1668) at the urging of his student Walda Heywat.
- **The Ark.** At Aksum, in the cathedral Fasilides rebuilt, one monk keeps the Ark of the Covenant, which the *Kebra Nagast* says Menelik, son of Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, brought home. Appointed for life by his predecessor, he alone may see it, and he never leaves its grounds.
- **Unction or union.** Gojjam's monks say Christ became Son of God by the Spirit's anointing; Debre Libanos says the union of natures was the anointing. The Lasta clergy hold a third view. It will take councils, excommunications and a ravaged province, and it won't stay settled.
- **The nuns.** Walatta Petros's communities, who outlasted the Jesuits, are composing her Life aloud; it will be written down in 1672.
- **The Oromo frontier.** Yohannes is fortifying Gojjam against the Oromo, with Oromo soldiers in his army.
- **The Siddis.** An African-descended dynasty from the Horn holds the island fortress of Janjira, off the Konkan coast, against Shivaji's yearly attacks; since 1661 its fleet has served the Mughals (see the Mughal India section).
- **Oman,** which took Muscat from the Portuguese in 1650, is raiding the Swahili coast (see the Indian Ocean section).

> **Further in:** Yohannes marries Sabla Wangel in October. In 1678 the Abuna will dissolve the marriage for incest.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The port.** Fasilides and the Yemeni imam tried to open **Beilul**, south of Ottoman Massawa, as Ethiopia's own outlet to the sea, and gave it up. Someone wants to try again, and the naib of Arkiko would rather they didn't.
- **The list.** A party member is a Muslim, a "Frank" or a foreigner, and the council's rulings just reached their door.
- **The keeper.** A stranger has come to Aksum asking to see the Ark. The keeper can't leave its grounds to find out why.
- **The handover.** An Oromo class's eight years are ending, and the next class's men take power on schedule. Someone in Gondar thinks the change is an opening.
- **Harar besieged.** Raiders at the gate, a qadi dead or missing, and a city of shrines that needs someone to get a message out.
- **The holy man.** A Funj saint mocks Badi II to his face, and his poems curse rulers who break their word. The sultan wants him silenced. (His model: Farah Wad Taktouk, who answered a sultan's order to teach his camel to read with a verse about death.)
- **The wrong name in red.** A däbtära's scroll, the height of a man, came back with someone else's name on it.
- **Buda.** A Beta Israel mason is accused after a child sickens. The party has a day to show what really happened.
- **Wehni.** A prince on the prison mountain has a friend at court.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
Mughal India is the richest state in the world: by Scott's figure, about a quarter of the world's output. In 1668 the emperor Aurangzeb is ten years into his reign, the empire is near its greatest extent, and the Europeans hold a few factories in other people's ports.

**The one thing to remember:** in India the Europeans are tenants. The landlord is pious, and he licenses magic the way he enforces prayer. His real trouble isn't at sea. It's in the Deccan hills, where a Maratha raja who escaped his court in 1666 is building a kingdom.

> **Further in:** some of the yogis whose arts the emperor regulates hold their land by Mughal grant, and their order is older than his dynasty.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
India is not one landscape: the highest mountains on earth, a true desert, a dry plateau, a rainforest coast and the world's largest mangrove forest.

- **The monsoon** brings most of the year's rain in summer. When the rains fail, famine follows, and plague follows famine; the Deccan and Gujarat famine of 1630–32 is within living memory.
- **The Gangetic plain** is the heart of Mughal farming. Bengal, at its eastern end, is rich in rice, cloth and silk. Arakanese and Portuguese pirates raided its coast for slaves until Shaista Khan took Chittagong in 1666 and freed thousands of captives.
- **The Deccan** is a high, dry plateau behind the Western Ghats, whose Malabar coast grows pepper.
- **The Thar** is sand hills the monsoon passes by. Its herders move with the rains, so the setting's Hidden "at the edge of the village" doesn't fit: herders have no fixed edge.
- **The Himalaya.** At their foot runs the Terai, marsh so malarial it works as a wall against armies; only the Tharu live in it well. Above, the Kathmandu Valley holds three rival Newar kingdoms.
- **The Sundarbans**, at the Ganges mouth, are tidal mangrove and man-eating tigers.
- **Animals.** Lions live across the north. Akbar once kept a thousand trained cheetahs.
- **Disease.** Plague, smallpox and fevers are endemic. Healing magic tempers an outbreak, but healers are few, so it softens an epidemic and can't stop one (Scott).
- **New things.** Chilies came with the Portuguese; by 1668 the hookah is everywhere.

> *"The English write 'the Indies' as if it were one country. I have walked from the snow to the salt, and it was never one country."* (a Nath yogi at Surat)

> **Further in:** the drought record for India after 1640 is thin. Mostly kind. Lean years still come, but food goes further in Euphonia (see Magic in Daily Life), so a lean year is hungry rather than deadly.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The emperor.** Aurangzeb (Alamgir) won the throne in a war of succession in 1658 and deposed his father, Shah Jahan, builder of the Taj Mahal. His court is religious-minded and regulates magic (Scott). His great-grandfather Akbar ran the opposite court, with weekly debates among scholars of every faith. The *muhtasib*, each city's censor of public morals, polices magic under Islamic law, and the great law book Aurangzeb has commissioned, the *Fatawa-e-Alamgiri*, will set the rules down.
- **A conquering dynasty.** The Mughals came from Central Asia in 1526 and rule conquered peoples: Rajput houses bound by marriage, a Sikh community whose fifth Guru was executed under Jahangir, and a mostly Hindu population under a Muslim court. Their rivals are conquerors too: the Deccan sultans sacked Vijayanagara for good in 1565.
- **The Deccan sultanates.** Bijapur and Golconda still stand, with courts of Persian, Central Asian, African and Indian elites. Golconda's mines are virtually the world's only source of diamonds.
- **The Marathas.** Shivaji killed Bijapur's general in 1659, sacked Surat in 1664, and escaped Aurangzeb's court in 1666. He isn't crowned yet.
- **The money.** Gujarati merchants finance much of the ocean's trade by *hundi*, the bill of exchange. Mutapa's House of the Bird learned credit from them.
- **The companies.** The English have factories at Surat and Madras; the Dutch trade here too; the French arrive this year. All hold their posts on Mughal or local sufferance. European territorial rule is ninety years off.
- **The mountains.** Pratap Malla rules Kathmandu and mints coin for Tibet.

> **Further in:** Golconda's diamonds are the stone every crown wants. Nobody has asked whether a diamond does for some art what platinum does for Mutapa's.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
The Mughal court regulates magic (Scott). Under Aurangzeb that means a permit, a patron or a pious reason.

- **Learned magic.** The Islamic world's learned magic is Hermeticism too, shaped by Arabic scholarship (Scott). Its science of letters and talismans gets its own treatment rather than a reskin.
- **Wisdom.** Holiness works for anyone actually holy (Scott): a Sufi at his shrine, a Brahman priest, a village goddess's non-Brahman priest, a Sikh. Possession is central: in Kerala's *teyyam*, Dalit and tribal performers become the god.
- **The Sandhyānāthāha** are the Naths (Scott): a Shaiva order blending hatha yoga with alchemy in pursuit of a perfected, immortal body. Initiates split their ears for great earrings. Kings and commoners honor them warily for fear of their curses; folk belief credits them with weather control, changing size, exorcism, healing, flight and necromancy, and in Euphonia those powers are real.
  - Many are married householders who take a share of the harvest for keeping off locusts; some are warrior ascetics. Their establishments hold Mughal grants.
  - In 1668 the order is taking shape. Mostly they don't. They keep to their pilgrim roads and cave shrines, and the world comes to them there: a raja who wants to live forever, or a dying man who wants one more year.
- **Mutapan curiosities** reach Surat on the Monsoon Road. A Mughal noble with a self-lighting lamp is making the same statement as the Viennese lady.

> **Further in:** that Aurangzeb asked the Nath abbot of Jakhbar for an alchemical mercury preparation is often reported (unverified). Gorakhnath, refused alms in Patan, sat on the valley's rain-serpents until it stopped raining; the king had to send to Assam for his teacher to make him get up.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
South Asia's spirits belong to living religions. Much of the record of village belief comes from 19th-century British officials and missionaries, who called non-Brahman worship "demonolatry," and many possession traditions are carried by Dalit and Adivasi communities.

- **The pari.** The Persian and Urdu word for fairy, and the Mughal court's own Hidden: beautiful, morally mixed, Muslim or not. Paris carry people off to Paristan, sometimes to a pari wedding, in body or in trance. Marriages between paris and men go badly.
- **Yakshas and yakshis.** Spirits of trees, lakes and towns, guardians of buried treasure. Kerala's yakshi waits in the *pala* tree for night travelers (that version was written down from 1909).
- **Nagas.** Serpent people with jeweled palaces under the earth and waters. They hold the rain. Royal houses claim descent from a nagini.
- **The ban jhakri.** A small, backward-footed forest shaman in Nepal who takes pure-hearted boys, teaches them drums and healing, and returns them as shamans. His consort would eat them if he let her. (20th-century ethnography.) In Euphonia that may be a Revelator's calling.
- **The acheri.** In Kumaon, ghosts of girls who died violently revel on the peaks at dusk; meeting one can kill. A red thread at the throat protects. (19th-century colonial sources.)
- **The village guardians.** *Gramadevata*, often goddesses, both send epidemics and stop them. Exorcists (*ojha*) treat the possessed. These are the Hidden Killers' nearest kin here.
- **Bonbibi.** The Sundarbans' forest guardian, honored by Hindus and Muslims, against the tiger-king Dakshin Ray. Dakshin Ray's worship is attested by 1686; Bonbibi's own text is 19th-century.
- **Where the comparison breaks.** Many of these are worshipped gods, not feared neighbors; many are the dead; and a South Asian spirit is more likely to enter a person than carry them off. The Wild Hunt rides here too, under its own names.

> **Further in:** Mughal painters put paris at the emperor's elbow.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Bombay**, Catherine of Braganza's dowry to Charles II, passes to the English East India Company.
- **The French** are new in Surat and looking for a port of their own.
- **The Deccan.** Shivaji is home from Agra. Bijapur and Golconda stand between him and the Mughals.
- **Bengal.** Shaista Khan holds Chittagong, and the delta's emptied coast is being resettled.
- **The platinum rush.** Every power's agents are on the Monsoon Road, and Surat is where they change ships.
- **Kathmandu.** In our history Pratap Malla builds the Rani Pokhari in 1670 for his grieving queen, with water said to come from 51 sacred rivers.

> **Further in:** in our history Shivaji was crowned in 1674, and the Mughals spent the rest of Aurangzeb's life fighting in the Deccan.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **A warehouse in Surat.** The last time the Marathas came, they sacked the city. This time a factory holds a crate of Mutapan curiosities.
- **A license.** A Company factor needs the court's permission for something his employers won't name.
- **A curse.** A Nath yogi refused alms in a Company town.
- **Golconda.** A foreign natural philosopher wants to test a diamond the sultan won't sell.
- **A pari wedding.** A groom went to one and hasn't come back.
- **Bengal's captives.** The slavers lost Chittagong. They didn't lose their ships.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
The far south is a crowd of heirs. Vijayanagara broke a century ago, and its old governors are kings now: the Nayaks of Madurai and Thanjavur, the Setupatis of Ramnad, the Wodeyars of Mysore, the Nayakas of Keladi. They fight every season over the Kaveri's rice, while Bijapur's captains hold the northern forts and Golconda's run the coast. Below the Ghats, Kerala is a patchwork of kingdoms where descent runs through women. Along both coasts the Dutch have just thrown out the Portuguese, and they mean to own the pepper.

**The one thing to remember:** the last Vijayanagara emperor is still alive in 1668, a guest of his former vassals, and every king in the south claims to act in his name when it suits. The empire is a ghost everyone salutes. What actually rules is the price of cloth and rice.

> **Further in:** follow the cloth. Coromandel's painted cottons buy the cloves and nutmeg of the islands, and in famine years the Dutch ship the people who paint them to Batavia (see Southeast Asia). North, Golconda's diamonds and Shivaji's family lands run up into the Deccan (see Mughal India). Across Rama's Bridge lies Ceylon, under the same monsoon and over the same deep (see the Indian Ocean). Malabar's pepper has sailed to the Red Sea for a thousand years (see the Horn and the Nile), and Mutapan buyers come up the same road looking for stones (see Mutapa).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Three countries share one tip of India: the dry Tamil plain, the rain-forest Ghats, and Kerala's green strip between hills and sea.

- **Two monsoons.** Malabar gets the southwest rains from June; the Coromandel coast, in the Ghats' rain shadow, waits for the northeast monsoon, October to December (general knowledge). Either one failing is a famine.
- **The Kaveri delta** is the rice bowl, watered by channels a thousand years old. Thanjavur sits on it, and everyone else wants it.
- **Temple cities.** Madurai's Meenakshi temple, Srirangam's seven walls on a Kaveri island, Chidambaram's dancing Shiva, Rameswaram at the land's end. Each is a landlord, a bank, an employer and a festival calendar.
- **The Ghats** are pepper and cardamom gardens, worked by hill peoples who know them as home.
- **Kerala has no village edge.** Houses stand in their own compounds among rice, coconut and backwater; the edge is each household's sacred grove (*kavu*) and snake grove.
- **The pearl coast.** In the Gulf of Mannar the Catholic Paravar fishers dive for pearls and chank shell. The shoals to Ceylon are the Ramayana's bridge, and the Setupati is its lord.
- **Hunger.** The Coromandel coast failed again and again in the 1640s–60s. Magic stretches food where a caster stands (see Magic in Daily Life); most villages have none.

> *"The Dutch ask which king owns this road. Ask which god it belongs to, and which poligar collects on it this month."* (a pilgrims' guide at Rameswaram)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Every crown here is a conqueror's heir, and every king's army is the sum of his lords' loyalties.

- **Madurai.** **Chokkanatha Nayak**, about twenty-two, has moved his capital north to the Rock Fort at Tiruchirappalli (1665 is the date usually given (unverified)), stripping, the British later said, his grandfather's carved palace to build it. Mysore beat him at **Erode** in 1667, and he pays tribute to Bijapur. His seventy-two *palayakkarar* (poligars) each police a district and keep troops on a third of its revenue, and they are deciding whom to obey.
- **Thanjavur.** Old **Vijayaraghava Nayak** has held the delta since 1634, writes Telugu poems, patronizes music, and is broke. He has been at war with his Danish tenants since 1655 over the rent.
- **Ramnad.** The **Setupati** ("lord of the bridge") guards the pilgrim road to Rameswaram with Maravar soldiers. He is Madurai's man in theory and his own in practice; one list gives Tirumalai Raghunatha Setupati for 1668. His ports are Muslim merchant towns.
- **Mysore.** **Devaraja Wodeyar I** has renounced Vijayanagara and declared himself sovereign; his nephew **Chikkadevaraja**, who won at Erode, is twenty-three and learned. In living memory Mysore's general cut off civilians' noses, and Madurai answered in kind.
- **Keladi.** The Veerashaiva Nayakas of the western hills grow rich on pepper and took the Portuguese coastal forts. **Somashekara Nayaka I** rules; his wife **Chennamma** will rule after him for twenty-five years.
- **The emperor without an empire.** **Sriranga III** lives under Keladi's protection, still hoping to retake Vellore. He rode with Madurai at Erode and lost.
- **The sultans' south.** Bijapur holds **Gingee** and Vellore through Maratha captains: Shivaji's father held Bangalore until he died in 1664, and his half-brother **Venkoji** succeeds him there. Golconda holds the coast to San Thome (see Mughal India).
- **Kerala's kings.** The **Zamorin** of Calicut is the strongest. The **Raja of Cochin** is a Dutch protectorate in practice (general knowledge). In **Venad** the king shares power with the "lords of the eight houses," and the **queens of Attingal** hold their own land and warriors. Most ruling houses and the Nair soldiery reckon descent through women: kings are succeeded by their sisters' sons (general knowledge).
- **The Europeans** are tenants on the coast. The **Dutch** took Nagapattinam, the pearl fishery, Cochin, Quilon, Cranganore and Cannanore between 1658 and 1663, and run it all from Pulicat. The **English** hold Madras, the **Danes** Tranquebar. The **French** open their first Indian factory this year, at Surat.

> **Further in:** in our history Chokkanatha takes Thanjavur in 1673 and the old king dies in his palace; then Bijapur's Maratha general takes it from both of them and founds a dynasty that lasts to 1855.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Holiness works for anyone actually holy (Scott), and this region is crowded with the holy: Saiva and Vaishnava, Jain, Muslim, three kinds of Christian and two kinds of Jew, within a week's walk.

- **The temples are power.** A Nayak who builds a pillared hall at Madurai is buying legitimacy as well as merit; the priests, musicians, temple dancers (*devadasi*) and accountants serve the god as a household.
- **Kalaripayattu.** Nair and Thiyya fighters train in the *kalari* from childhood under a *gurukkal*, who teaches the vital points (*marmam*) only to his most trusted pupils. Disputes that assemblies can't settle go to a formal combat, often fought by hired champions.
- **Physicians of the palm leaf.** Kerala's healers keep their knowledge in family palm-leaf books, and an Ezhava physician's family library knows more plants than any garden in Europe. Knowledge is universal: this is medicine and natural history, not mystic lore.
- **The *mantravadi*** is Kerala's exorcist and sorcerer.
- **The Mappila scholars** of Ponnani keep the Islamic world's learned magic, which is Hermeticism too (Scott). Their jinn are what Islam says they are.
- **The Jesuits in saffron.** The Madurai Mission's priests live as Indian renunciants and win converts mostly among non-Brahman castes. Their prayers work exactly as well as those of the Saiva polemicists who preach against them.
- **Two bishops, one church.** The St Thomas Christians are freshly split between Rome and Antioch.
- **The god in person.** In north Kerala's **theyyam**, a performer from a hereditary community puts on the god's face and becomes the god, and blesses and judges the worshippers to their faces. No source describes it before 1668 (unverified): likely, but undocumented. On the Kanara coast the **bhutas** of bhuta kola are land-spirits and judges whose rulings through a medium can't be appealed (unverified for 1668). Both are gods and the deified dead, not the Hidden.

> **Further in:** in our history the Ezhava physician **Itty Achuden** dictates his family's books for the Dutch *Hortus Malabaricus* (Amsterdam, 1678 onward), with three Konkani Brahman physicians checking him. Its real authors are Indian, and in 1668 nobody has asked them yet.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Most of what we know about village religion here was written down by 19th-century British officials and 20th-century anthropologists. The far south has an older witness: Tamil poetry of the first centuries CE.

- **The *cur*.** Sangam poetry knows *ananku*, a formless power felt as fear, dwelling in mountains, forests, trees and waters, and the ***cur*** and the "*cur* women," frightening beings of devastating force who live where it lives. They are nobody's dead and nobody's temple gods. In Euphonia they are the Tamil Hidden, the high Hidden of the hills past the fields.
- **The Velan, the oldest go-between.** When a girl wastes away, her family calls the Velan, who dances the *veriyattu*, is possessed, and says what has seized her; in the poems she is in love with a man from the hills (general knowledge of the poems, not checked). In Euphonia the man from the hills may not be a man.
- **The yakshi.** On Kerala's night roads a beautiful woman waits in the *pala* tree. The versions in print (from 1909) make her a wronged dead woman, which the Hidden are not. In Euphonia some Hidden took the yakshi's name, as others took the jinn's, and folk memory later gave them dead women's stories.
- **Chathan's imitators.** Chathan is a worshipped guardian god in Malabar (unverified before 1925). The household nuisances that set clothes alight, throw stones and turn beds to thorns, and stop when fed, are low Hidden who took his name.
- **Ayyanar's night patrol.** Ayyanar is a god, not the Hidden. His shrine stands at the village boundary, villagers give him terracotta horses, some taller than a man, to ride his **night-time patrols**, and his black-faced watchman **Karuppan** takes the blood offerings the god won't. This is the region's answer to the Hidden Killers: the god himself rides the boundary. (The horse offering is documented in modern sources; its age is (unverified).)
- **Not the Hidden:** Ayyanar, Karuppan and Mariamman (gods); the theyyam deities and bhutas (gods and the deified dead); the snake groves' nagas, kin to the deep (Scott; see the Indian Ocean); the jinn.
- **Where the comparison breaks.** A spirit here is likelier to enter a person than carry them off, and a hereditary specialist performs the cure in public. The taken are usually the possessed, and they come back.
- **The raiding season.** The south keeps the northern dark half, mildly, and it opens with the northeast monsoon. Theyyam's season, late October to May, matches it almost exactly.

> **Further in:** no one may appeal a bhuta's ruling.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The man who wouldn't leave.** **Sir Edward Winter**, Madras's dismissed agent, has held Fort St George since late 1665 with his successor in the cells, writing to the King that he is a Royalist against a Puritan. Two Company ships arrive on 21 May; he surrenders on **22 May**.
- **The fort nobody remembered.** At Tranquebar, Governor **Eskild Andersen Kongsbakke** has held a walled Danish town for thirteen years against Thanjavur with local soldiers, Portuguese mercenaries and privateering. No ship has come from Denmark in a quarter-century; one will arrive in May 1669.
- **The oath on the rope.** In 1653 the St Thomas Christians held a rope tied to a cross and swore off Portuguese church authority. Now their churches are split between a bishop consecrated for Rome in 1663 and their archdeacon, **Mar Thoma I**, confirmed by **Gregorios**, a Syriac bishop who landed from Antioch's patriarch in 1665. The Dutch have expelled the Portuguese clergy.
- **Back from the hills.** In 1662 the Portuguese at Cochin blamed the Jews for a Dutch attack, burned their synagogue with its scrolls and sacked Jew Town; the community hid in the hills nearly a year. Under the Dutch they are home, rebuilding, short of books.
- **The famine's trade.** In 1663 the cloth painters of Nagapattinam sold themselves into slavery to eat. By one count 8,000 to 10,000 people were shipped from this coast in 1659–61, mostly through Pulicat, where a child sold for four guilders in a famine year. The ships still sail for Batavia.

> **Further in:** the Mamankam fair comes every twelve years; the next is perhaps **1671** (unverified; extrapolated). Its *chavers*, from four Nair families, are sworn to break through the Zamorin's guard and kill him, or die. In 1695 a sixteen-year-old reaches him, and the Zamorin dodges.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Before the ships.** It is early 1668 at Fort St George. Winter holds the gate, his successor is in the cells, and the Sultan of Golconda hasn't decided whose side to take.
- **Tranquebar's rent.** Thanjavur's men are at the walls again, and the governor needs one more privateering cruise to pay his soldiers.
- **The painter for sale.** On a Batavia-bound ship out of Pulicat is someone who can paint any pattern on cloth, and someone who owes them.
- **The emperor's seal.** Sriranga III has nothing left to give but legitimacy, and three kings want to borrow it.
- **The noseless veteran** of the war of noses wants a surgeon who can rebuild his face. The operation goes back to Sushruta; who practices it in 1668 is (unverified).
- **The wasting girl.** A family in the Madurai hills called the Velan. He came out of the dance and won't say what he saw.
- **The sworn-to-die.** A Nair youth is training for a Mamankam three years off, and his family wants him to live.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
The Indian Ocean is the world's busiest sea, and it runs on a timetable: the monsoon blows one way for half the year and the other way for the other half. Europeans hold forts on its shores (a fading Portuguese string, a growing Dutch one, a few English), but not the sea. Asian, Arab and Swahili ships work it too, and Mutapa now holds its southern gate.

**The one thing to remember:** the ocean isn't a frontier. It's a market with a timetable, and everyone waits on the same wind. In 1668 the platinum rush has put every power's agents on that road. Under it, in the deep, is something none of them have charted.

> **Further in:** the Hidden have built a civilization in the deepest parts of this ocean (Scott). The sailors of every shore have a story about who lives under the water.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Sea
sections.text:
- **The monsoon.** The southwest monsoon blows in off the ocean in northern summer; dry northeast winds blow out to sea in winter. Dhows sail to East Africa on the northeast monsoon and come back to Arabia in late spring. At the southwest monsoon's height, roughly June to August, much of India's west coast is closed to shipping (unverified). A ship that misses the wind waits months for the next one.
- **The eastern seas** keep the same calendar. The Manila galleon sails once a year each way across the Pacific, Mexican silver west and Chinese silk east.
- **Coral and mangrove.** The Swahili towns are built of coral stone. Mangrove poles go north by dhow to the treeless Persian Gulf.
- **The ships.** Dhow planks are sewn with coconut-fiber rope, not nailed; junks and European ships share the routes.
- **The spices grow in tiny places.** Pepper comes from Malabar and Sumatra. The Dutch restrict cloves to Ambon and Ternate. Nutmeg and mace come from the Banda Islands, which the Dutch conquered in 1621: of some 13,000–15,000 people, about 1,000 survived as forced laborers, and the nutmeg trees were divided into plots worked by slaves. Coffee grows commercially only in Yemen and ships from Mocha (unverified).
- **The islands.** Socotra is this ocean's Galápagos, cut off by wind from June to September. The dodo of Mauritius is nearly or entirely gone, eaten by sailors and their pigs and rats.
- **Disease** travels with the ships. Healing magic tempers an outbreak, but healers are few, so it softens an epidemic and can't stop one (Scott).

> *"You don't sail when you want. You sail when the sea says. The Franks never learned it. They learned to wait in forts."* (a Gujarati captain at Mocha)

> **Further in:** medieval travelers credited Socotra's people with sorcery over the winds, and the island is shut by the wind four months a year.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Shore by shore, west to east:

- **Mutapa** holds the southern gate: Sofala's gold and the Cape every European fleet must pass. See the Mutapa section.
- **The Swahili city-states.** Kilwa, Mombasa, Malindi, Pate and Zanzibar are Muslim towns living on trade between the interior and the sea. Each picked a foreign patron: Malindi chose Portugal; Mombasa turned to the Ottomans and later Oman.
- **The Portuguese** hold Mozambique Island, Fort Jesus at Mombasa, Goa and Macau. They have lost Hormuz, Malacca and Muscat.
- **Oman.** The Ya'rubi imams drove the Portuguese from Muscat, are building a navy, and raid Portuguese posts down the Swahili coast.
- **Sri Lanka.** The king of Kandy holds the highlands; the Dutch hold the cinnamon coast, taken from the Portuguese.
- **Aceh**, in northern Sumatra, controls pepper and once asked the Ottomans for cannon-makers.
- **The Dutch East India Company** rules from Batavia and holds Malacca, Ambon and the Bandas. Its *hongi* fleets cut down spice trees outside its control.
- **Mataram** unified most of Java under Sultan Agung, who twice failed to take Batavia. Amangkurat I rules it now.
- **Johor** keeps the Orang Laut, the boat-dwelling sea people of the Riau islands, as its navy: they patrol the straits, fight pirates and guide traders.
- **Ayutthaya**, in Siam, has Japanese, Dutch and Portuguese quarters.
- **Spanish Manila** runs the galleon and the Philippines, where Spanish clergy persecute the *babaylan*, the old spirit-mediums. Babaylan led risings in 1621–22 and 1663.

The empires among them, Asian and European, all rule conquered peoples. The Bandanese have suffered the worst of it.

> **Further in:** in 1631 a sultan of Mombasa, raised Catholic as Dom Jerónimo, killed the Fort Jesus garrison; the Portuguese came back the next year. By its founding pact, every king of Mataram is the husband of the Queen of the Southern Sea. Batavia has made no pact with anyone in the water.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Most of the ocean's shores are Muslim, and the Islamic world's learned magic is Hermeticism too (Scott). The healers are professionals, with apprenticeships and specialties.

- **The Swahili *mganga*** is usually an older man: a healer of the book (Islamic texts), of the spirit, of the head or of plants.
- **The Malay *bomoh*** heals, reads the land and works sorcery; the ***pawang*** handles rites for weather, animals, the sea and the harvest. Their charms draw on Sanskrit mantras, local spirits, the gods and Allah together.
- **The Javanese *dukun*** heals with herbs, spells and offerings, blesses land and drives spirits out of people.
- **Sri Lanka's *tovil*** exorcists dance dusk to dawn against the eighteen *sanni*, each a demon of one disease.
- **The *babaylan*** of the Philippines were mostly women of high status, some called by illness or visions; the *asog*, men who lived as women, were shamans by being what they were.
- **Mutapan devices** come up the coast as cargo. So does platinum, and so, if anyone dares, do shewstones.
- **Navigation** is where natural philosophy proves itself: the Navigator doesn't ask the wind for favors.

> **Further in:** on the Swahili coast, some *jini* are kept in rooms, chests or bottles for their owners' gain, and demand blood. Not every device on this road that runs by itself is Mutapan.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
These are living traditions of peoples who are mostly Muslim or Christian and see their spirits as part of that faith. Apart from the Spanish Philippines, most of the record is 19th- and 20th-century, and reform movements condemn much of it.

- **The deep.** The Hidden have built their own undersea civilization in the deepest parts of the Indian Ocean (Scott). The nagas are always a possible threat there (Scott). The Swahili *jini* of the sea, Ratu Kidul's court and the nagas' palaces are one deep civilization, each shore with its own name for it. What the traders know: some waters take a toll, some ships come home with a stranger aboard, and a captain who refuses the toll doesn't sail that sea again. The record offers threads: Swahili *jini* are often said to live in the sea; Ratu Kidul rules the Southern Ocean off Java; South Asia's nagas keep palaces under the water.
- **The orang bunian**, the Malay world's "hidden people": near-human, with no groove above the upper lip, living in hills and forests with families, clans and kings. People ask leave before entering their places, and don't whistle in the forest, because the bunian may answer. They marry humans; a husband may come home to find everyone he knew dead.
- **Ratu Kidul**, Queen of the Southern Sea. Mataram's founder won her help on condition that he and all his descendants be her husbands. Green is her color; on the south coast people don't wear it near the water. She is a court institution, not peasant lore. (The chronicle survives in 18th-century versions.)
- **The engkanto** of the Philippines live in great trees like the *balete*, where those they favor see palaces. They lead travelers astray, cause fevers and madness, and father children with humans.
- **The Swahili spirits.** *Shetani*, *pepo* and *jini* possess people. The possession cults that settle them seek a lasting relationship with the spirit, not an expulsion.
- **The dead are separate.** The *pontianak*, ghost of a woman who died in childbirth, and the *penanggalan*, a witch whose head flies at night, belong to the dangers of childbirth, not to the Hidden.
- **The edge.** For the Orang Laut and the dhow crews there is no village edge; the edge is the deep water. Who keeps watch at it, and what the Wild Hunt looks like at sea, is open.

> **Further in:** the bunian keep their own kings. Nobody has asked whom those kings answer to.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Run.** The Treaty of Breda (1667) has just given the Dutch the nutmeg island of Run, after they cut down all its trees. Their hold on the Bandas is complete.
- **Oman** is raiding south, and Fort Jesus is watching the horizon.
- **Bombay** passes to the English East India Company.
- **The Visayas.** The Jesuit Alcina dates his account of the pre-Christian Visayas to this year, five years after a babaylan rising.
- **Kandy.** The Englishman Robert Knox has been the king's captive since 1660.
- **Taiwan and the China coast.** Koxinga's heirs hold Taiwan, and the Qing have emptied their own coast to starve them (see the East Asia section).
- **The platinum rush.** Every power's agents are on the Monsoon Road, looking for Mutapan metal and Mutapan secrets.

> **Further in:** in our history, a Greek adventurer runs Ayutthaya's foreign policy in the 1680s, until a palace coup.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The missed wind.** A ship that sailed late is stuck in port for a season, with a cargo everyone in town wants.
- **Seedlings.** Someone is offering nutmeg seedlings from outside the Dutch plots.
- **A bottled jini** for sale on the Swahili coast, and the blood it asks for.
- **A sailor who wore green** off Java's south coast.
- **A sounding line** that comes up wrong over the deep.
- **The Monsoon Road:** a ship, a cargo of curiosities, and an ocean of people who want to see inside one.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
River kingdoms on the mainland, port sultanates on the islands, the busiest straits in the world between. In 1668 Narai of Ayutthaya keeps the most cosmopolitan court in Asia, Burma has just handed the last Ming emperor to his killers, and two Vietnamese houses face each other across a pair of walls. In the islands the Dutch East India Company (VOC) is breaking the port powers one by one, and Makassar is still fighting a year after it signed the peace. Up the Mekong, monks and pilgrims walk the galleries of Angkor Wat, as they have for five hundred years.

**The one thing to remember:** the islands are losing a war one port at a time, and the mainland is winning its own. Above both stands Angkor: never lost, still holy, kept by the heirs of the people who built it.

> **Further in:** this is the middle of the Monsoon Road. West, Arakan and the Mughals meet at Chittagong (see Mughal India); the pepper and the monsoon run on to the Indian Ocean. North, the junks sail home to a coast the Qing have emptied (see East Asia). East, the Manila galleon crosses the Pacific by way of Guam (see Oceania). And the ring closes: Madagascar was settled from southeast Borneo, and Malagasy is an Austronesian language. Its coast faces Mutapa's (see Mutapa).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
River plains on the mainland, shallow seas in the islands, and the monsoon over all of it (see the Indian Ocean for the calendar). The northeast monsoon brings the Chinese junks south; the southwest takes them home.

- **The rivers make the kingdoms.** Burma lives on the Irrawaddy, Ayutthaya on the Chao Phraya, Lan Xang and Cambodia on the Mekong, the Trịnh north on the Red River. The Nguyễn south is a thin strip between mountains and sea.
- **Ayutthaya** is an island city 80 km upriver; a fleet at the river mouth shut it off in 1663.
- **The Tonle Sap** reverses its flow every wet season and fills the Great Lake, Angkor's lake (general knowledge, not checked).
- **The islands** are joined by their seas more than parted. The Orang Laut and the Sama-Bajau live on boats. Ternate is one volcano with a sultan's town at its foot (general knowledge, not checked).
- **Rice and sago.** Wet rice in the plains and on Java; sago in the eastern islands, where cutting down a village's sago is how the VOC starves it.
- **Disease** is malaria in the hills and smallpox in the ports. These peoples have shared Eurasia's diseases for centuries; there is no American-style collapse here.

None of it is empty. The forests of Arakan and Angkor are farmed, hunted, named and full of shrines.

> *"The Dutch ask how many soldiers our king has. Count the monks first."* (a Lao official at Vientiane)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Every empire here, Asian or European, holds conquered peoples: Ayutthaya took Chiang Mai in 1662–63, Gowa forced Islam on the Bugis by war, and the VOC empties whole islands.

**The river kings:**

- **Narai of Ayutthaya** (r. 1656–1688) won his throne on the Day of Ashura with Persian, Japanese and Dutch swords. His court holds Persian ministers, a Japanese quarter, Makassarese, Chinese, Dutch and French bishops.
- **Pye Min of Burma** (r. 1661–1672) took Ava from his brother, then survived a Qing army, a Mon revolt and a Siamese invasion in three years.
- **Đại Việt** is one kingdom in name and two in fact. The Lê emperor reigns at Thăng Long (Hanoi) as a figurehead for the **Trịnh** lord, Trịnh Tạc; the **Nguyễn** lord, Nguyễn Phúc Tần (general knowledge, not checked), rules the south from near Huế.
- **Cambodia** rules from **Oudong** under Barom Reachea V, whom a Nguyễn army installed in 1658 in place of a king who had become a sultan (his reign rests on one source). The price was land.
- **Lan Xang** under Sourigna Vongsa spends its wealth on monasteries, not guns. **Arakan**, a Buddhist kingdom with an Islamicate court, holds a murdered Mughal prince's treasure and lost Chittagong for it.

**The island powers:**

- **The VOC** rules from **Batavia**, a walled canal city. More than half its people are enslaved, bought at its market from Bali, Sulawesi, India and as far as Madagascar.
- **Amangkurat I of Mataram** rules inland Java from Plered. In 1648 he had 5,000–6,000 Islamic scholars and their families killed. His son, the crown prince, wants him gone.
- **Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa of Banten** is the VOC's rival on the water, with ships to Persia, Japan and Manila and letters to the king of Denmark.
- **Sultan Hasanuddin of Gowa** holds Makassar against the VOC and **Arung Palakka**, a Bugis prince fighting his old overlords for the Dutch.
- **Taj ul-Alam Safiatuddin of Aceh** (r. 1641–1675) is the first of four queens in a row. She has lost the pepper coast to the Dutch and kept Aceh free.
- **Ternate's** sultan takes 12,000 rijksdaalders a year to let the Dutch cut down his own clove trees.
- **Spanish Manila** runs the galleon. In June 1662, fearing Koxinga, it turned the guns of Intramuros on its own Chinese quarter, then pulled its garrisons out of the Moluccas and Mindanao.
- **The Moro sultanates** are unbeaten: Muhammad Kudarat of Maguindanao, nearly ninety, plays Dutch against Spanish, and Sulu's raiders are rising.
- **The smaller fires:** Johor, with the Orang Laut as its navy, at war with Jambi; Brunei at civil war since 1661, over a cockfight; the Catholic **Topasses** of Timor, who have beaten the Dutch four times and ignore Lisbon.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Holiness works for anyone actually holy, and this region is crowded with faiths, with older keepers of the land beneath them all.

- **Theravada kings** protect the monkhood, and their merit makes them legitimate. A Cleric here is most often a monk.
- **Aceh** is the archipelago's great school of Islam. A Gujarati Shaykh al-Islam burned a dead Sufi poet's books and left in 1644, out of the queen's favor; in 1661 **al-Singkili** came home from twenty years in Arabia, and will be the first to put the Qur'an into Malay. Learned magic in the Muslim ports is Hermeticism and the science of letters (Scott).
- **Đại Việt certifies its gods.** Village guardians are ranked by royal certificate (general knowledge, not checked), the way a ministry licenses a wizard. Legend says the court of these very years burned the temple of **Princess Liễu Hạnh**, the Mother Goddess, as an evil spirit, then rebuilt it and gave her a title when a plague struck the animals. (The written legend is 18th-century.)
- **The bissu** of the Bugis stand outside man and woman, speak with the gods and crown the kings of Bone.
- **The specialists:** Khmer *kru* treat spirit harm; Burmese *nat kadaw*, "spirit wives," are possessed at festivals; the *pawang* and *dukun* work as in the Indian Ocean section.

#### Angkor

Angkor Wat is one of the great holy places of the world, and it has never stopped being one.

- **A mountain of the gods.** Suryavarman II built it in the 12th century for Vishnu: a model of **Mount Meru**, the axis of the world, ringed by a moat for the cosmic ocean. Around it lie the Bayon's giant stone faces and the **barays**, reservoirs up to 7.8 km long that may have watered rice or may have stood for the oceans around Meru.
- **Never left.** Ayutthaya sacked the city in 1431, and the court moved downriver; its heirs rule at Oudong, a few days south. The temple stayed: its central shrine was filled with standing Buddhas, and it became a Theravada sanctuary.
- **Finished by its heirs.** Khmer kings came back in the 16th century and completed the reliefs Suryavarman's carvers had left undone, as their ancestors' work. In the gallery called the **Thousand Buddhas**, pilgrims have carved prayers since 1541.
- **The Japanese pilgrim.** In January 1632 Morimoto Ukondayū Kazufusa, who believed this was Jetavana, the Buddha's own garden, celebrated Khmer New Year here and left an inscription praying for his father and his dead mother. Three years later Japan forbade the journey.
- **Its own story.** The *Poem of Angkor Wat* (1620, or 1598) says Indra sent his architect **Preah Pisnukar** to build a palace on earth for his son. Cambodian builders still invoke Pisnukar as their patron. **Naga** line the causeways, and folk belief says naga and devas guard the temple.

**At the table.** Angkor doesn't check the label: it answered Vishnu's priests, it answers the Buddha's monks, and it answered a Japanese pilgrim who thought he was somewhere else.

-
-
-

> **Further in:** Pohnpei says two sorcerers raised Nan Madol by magic, and Euphonia says they did (see Oceania). Khmer tradition says Indra's architect raised Angkor. Here, hands built it, under Suryavarman II, and holiness came to live in it. A DM who wants the architect's story true can make it so.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The islands' Hidden are in the Indian Ocean section: the **orang bunian**, Ratu Kidul, the **engkanto**. Many Muslims now class them among the jinn; by Scott's test for the bori, they are Hidden that took the jinn's name. The mainland's Hidden have their own names, and nearly all the detail is 19th- and 20th-century ethnography.

- **The neak ta** guard Khmer places: a village, a great tree, a hill, a pond, sometimes an old Hindu god renamed. Until the 19th century, Khmer held that the land belonged to them. In Euphonia they are the Hidden who made terms: a spirit house, offerings, and a district to keep.
- **The phi.** The Thai and Lao village **phi ban** and the city pillar's guardian are Hidden on terms like the neak ta; the **phi pop**, which possesses and devours, is the Hidden off the leash.
- **The khwan.** Every body has thirty-two souls that can wander, and the *baci* rite calls them back. In Euphonia a wandered khwan is what the Hidden take, and a baci is how a family asks for it back.
- **The naga.** Khmer kings trace their line to a naga princess (general knowledge, not checked); whether Angkor's naga are kin to the nagas of the deep (Scott; see the Indian Ocean) is open.
- **Not the Hidden:** Burma's **nats**, mostly the violently dead who never left (the blacksmith of Tagaung, burned alive by a jealous king, is the nat of **Mount Popa**); Liễu Hạnh, who is a goddess; and the hantu and pontianak, who are the dead.
- **The line through the middle.** In the tropics the Wild Hunt keeps each hemisphere's calendar, milder. The equator runs through Sumatra and Borneo, so Aceh's Hunt rides in the northern dark half and Mataram's in the southern.
- **The Killers' kin** are the Khmer *kru* and the Malay *pawang*.

> **Further in:** every king of Mataram is the husband of the Queen of the Southern Sea. In 1668 that is Amangkurat I.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Makassar burns.** Hasanuddin signed the Treaty of Bongaya in November 1667, felt cheated, and went back to war. On 12 October the VOC and its Bugis allies win a great battle under the walls. The brick fortress of **Somba Opu** still stands.
- **Narai's elephants.** A letter from the king of Siam reaches Batavia on 1 December with four elephants and a request for craftsmen and European gadgets. Five years after the blockade, it's business as usual.
- **The walls are quiet.** The two Nguyễn walls near Đồng Hới have held for a generation against everything the Trịnh could send. The Nguyễn buy cannon through Portuguese Macau.
- **Banten's new judge.** **Yusuf of Makassar**, nephew of Gowa's sultan, back from twenty years in Arabia, is Sultan Ageng's son-in-law and chief judge. His uncle's kingdom is dying as he watches.
- **Mataram waits.** The crown prince has rebelled once already. **Trunajaya**, a Madurese prince whose father the king executed, is growing up at court.
- **The delta.** Vietnamese settlers are moving onto Khmer land, and the Khmer are burning them out.
- **Aceh** is sending preachers to Siam, and the French are training Asian priests there.
- **The Moluccas** are the VOC's. Some 12,000 people of Hoamoal were moved off their land in 1656, and Banda's survivors live in Kei and Seram.

> **Further in:** in our history a mine breaches Somba Opu in June 1669, and the Makassarese scatter across the archipelago with nothing to lose. Here, the walls are standing.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The last sortie.** Somba Opu needs a message, or a prince, got out through the Bugis lines.
- **The emperor's seal.** A Ming loyalist who survived Burma's massacre of the Yongli court is selling something in an Ava market.
- **The walls.** A Trịnh spy wants a plan of the Nguyễn defenses, and a Macau gunfounder has one.
- **Shah Shuja's gold,** his missing daughters, and a Mughal governor at Chittagong who still wants the king who killed his emperor's brother.
- **The burned temple.** A village near the goddess's ruined shrine has started losing its animals.
- **The crown prince** of Mataram is recruiting, quietly. His father has the Queen of the Southern Sea; he needs someone else.
- **Batavia's market.** Someone a party member knows is for sale.
- **The exile.** A Japanese elder in Ayutthaya wants to die at home, and the shogun's law kills anyone who returns.
- **The pilgrim.** Carry an offering to Angkor for someone who can't make the journey.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
Qing China is a new dynasty still finishing its conquest. The Manchus took Beijing in 1644. In 1668 the emperor is fourteen, Ming loyalists hold Taiwan, three Chinese generals rule the south as near-kingdoms, and the government has emptied its own southeast coast to starve the loyalists out. Korea has been a Qing tributary since 1637. Japan has shut its doors.

**The one thing to remember:** in East Asia magic is a branch of government. The calendar is state business, the gods keep files on the dead, and a governor can close a temple. In December 1668 the emperor is going to test whose sky is right.

> **Further in:** the Qing's Astronomical Bureau chooses the days for burials. Someone chose the day each Ming prince's tomb was sealed.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **China is not one landscape:** loess plateau, flood-prone northern plain, the rice and silk country of the lower Yangtze, the tower karst of the southwest.
- **The Yellow River** runs south of Shandong, not where it does now. In 1642, during a rebel siege, its dikes were cut at Kaifeng, drowning most of the city.
- **The drought.** The late-Ming drought of 1637–43 was China's worst in a thousand years and helped bring the dynasty down. 1668 inherits a depopulated north.
- **The emptied coast.** Since 1661 the Qing have forced the people of the southeast coast inland, a strip about 25–30 km deep, to starve Koxinga's heirs of supplies. Ruined villages and watch-posts mark the line.
- **Tigers** live at every latitude; near Hangzhou a monk once held rites to pacify them.
- **The southwest** is home to the Miao, Yao, Zhuang and other non-Han peoples, only partly under Qing control. Han settlers called it "wild." It's someone's home.
- **New crops.** Maize, peanuts and sweet potatoes are spreading.
- **Korea** is a mountain peninsula. Tigers come close enough to Seoul that roads need armed escorts. Cattle plague has cycled through the herds since 1636.
- **Disease.** Healing magic tempers an epidemic, but healers are few, so it softens an outbreak and can't stop one (Scott).

> **Further in:** in our history, Korea's worst famine begins in 1670: frost, hail, then smallpox, measles and cattle plague.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Kangxi Emperor**, on the throne since 1661. The regent Oboi's faction still dominates the court; Kangxi has yet to break it. He is skeptical of elixirs and prefers to test claims.
- **The conquest.** The Manchus rule a Han majority, whose men wear the Manchu queue. Ming loyalists who won't serve have withdrawn into the mountains, some in Daoist dress.
- **The Three Feudatories.** Three former Ming generals hold the south as near-autonomous fiefs: Wu Sangui in Yunnan, Shang Kexi in Guangdong, Geng Jingzhong in Fujian.
- **Koxinga's heirs.** Zheng Chenggong, Koxinga, drove the Dutch from Taiwan in 1662 and died that year. His heirs rule the island as the Kingdom of Tungning.
- **The foreigners.** The Portuguese hold Macau. The Jesuits want their Bureau back. Russians are on the Amur.
- **Joseon Korea** is a Neo-Confucian state run by a scholar-official aristocracy, the *yangban*, under King Hyeonjong. Since its king kowtowed in 1637, Korea pays tribute to a dynasty its scholars consider barbarian.

> **Further in:** Koxinga was born in Hirado to a Japanese mother. The man who drove the Dutch out of Taiwan was born in Japan.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **The Astronomical Bureau** is China's ministry of magic (Scott). It makes the calendar, reads omens as comments on the emperor's rule, sites imperial tombs, and chooses the days for ceremonies, campaigns and burials. In 1664 the official Yang Guangxian had the Jesuit director Schall condemned, partly for choosing an inauspicious burial date for a prince.
- **The gods keep files.** Every walled city has a city god, a spirit-magistrate with whom families register a death.
- **Daoist priests.** The Zhengyi are married householders who do communal ritual, talismans, exorcism and healing, ordained under the Celestial Master at Mount Longhu. The Quanzhen are celibate monks practicing internal alchemy; their Longmen branch is reviving under Wang Changyue.
- **Learned magic.** Daoist talisman-writing gets its own school, not a Hermetic reskin (Scott).
- **The law.** The Qing Code has a statute against "sorcerers and heterodox arts." Unlicensed magic is the crime here too.
- **The Qiu Xian Zhe** are the fallen court alchemists (Scott). They lost their honors in 1567; in the Red Pill Case of 1620, an emperor died the morning after taking mineral pills; after 1644 they withdrew to the hills. 1668 is a low point. Their pattern is to fall from power and come back. The elixir, as always. They believe the old imperial tombs hold the recipes their predecessors were disgraced for, and 1668 is a cheap year to dig, with the new dynasty watching rebels, not graves.
- **Korea.** The *mudang*, mostly women, mediate between their clients and the spirits. The Neo-Confucian state taxes and despises them, and people still call them in a crisis.

> **Further in:** mineral elixirs were discredited by the emperors they killed. Nobody has shown they stopped being made.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
These are living religions, practiced today in China, Korea and the diaspora. Much of what's "known" comes from literati story collections and later folklorists, not from practitioners.

- **Fox spirits.** The *huli jing* is a seducer or a devoted wife, a trickster or a model of virtue. In north China foxes are worshipped at household altars and speak through mediums, mostly women. A fox takes human form at fifty and becomes a heavenly fox at a thousand. They may be China's high Hidden.
- **The Wutong.** Five sinister, often one-legged gods of Jiangnan, the closest Chinese match to the dangerous fair folk. They come as handsome gentlemen, seduce or possess women, and give husbands sudden wealth in exchange for their wives, then take it back at any slight.
- **The *shanxiao*.** One-legged mountain imps, afraid of loud noise, fond of music. Han settlers made the word a slur for their non-Han neighbors, so handle it with care.
- **The Ghost Festival.** On the fifteenth of the seventh month the underworld's gates open, with lanterns on the rivers and offerings for the hungry dead. Whether that night opens the Hidden's doors too, as Samhain does, is open.
- **Not yet.** The hopping corpse, the *jiangshi*, is first recorded in the 1780s.
- **Korea's *dokkaebi*** arise when a spirit enters an old object, a broom or something stained with blood. They wrestle men, love buckwheat jelly, and bring luck, or fire and disease.
- **Called by illness.** A Korean *mudang* is chosen by *sinbyeong*, spirit illness, and cured by accepting the calling. That may be a Revelator's calling.
- **The Hidden Killers' kin** here are the Zhengyi exorcists and the monks who pacify tigers. The Wild Hunt rides here too.

> **Further in:** Pu Songling is writing his fox wives and fox households in the setting's own decade.

sections.heading: Japan, the Closed Country
sections.text:
Scott's note: Japan may be its own pocket universe in the middle of all this, and needs much more detail. Closing the country closes it to foreign magic too.

- **The record.** The Tokugawa shoguns rule from Edo. Christianity is banned; the Shimabara rising of 1637–38 was crushed with Dutch cannon. Overseas travel is forbidden. Trade runs through four gates only: Nagasaki (the Dutch on Dejima, and the Chinese), Tsushima (Korea), Satsuma (Ryukyu) and Matsumae (the Ainu).
- **The land.** Japan must feed and build from its own islands; castle-building stripped its forests. Edo burned in 1657 and has been rebuilt with firebreaks.
- **Ainu Mosir**, Hokkaido, is Ainu land, not a frontier. Bad exchange rates are pushing toward war; in our history Shakushain's War begins in 1669.
- **Magic.** *Onmyōdō*, the court art of calendar, divination and ritual, belongs to the heirs of Abe no Seimei, whose mother was said to be a fox. Village *yamabushi*, mountain ascetics, do prayers and exorcisms and quarrel with the onmyōji over who may divine. Walking *miko*, often blind, call the gods and the dead.
- **The Hidden.** Scott's Shinto name for the Hidden is *kakuriyo*, "the hidden world."
  - A child lost at dusk is searched for with drums and lanterns, then declared *kamikakushi*, "hidden by the kami": taken by a local god, a mountain man or a *tengu* dressed as a yamabushi.
  - Foxes are Inari's messengers and possess young women. A *kappa* in 1668 is a hairy, ape-like river thing that drowns horses and children. Wolves are gods of the fields.
  - There are Japanese high elves (Scott).
- **How it might be a pocket universe**:
  - The closing is a ward as well as a law: foreign magic dims inside it.
  - Japan's Hidden are sealed in with the Japanese, so *kakuriyo* has a tide of its own.
  - The four gates are the only doors, for spirits as for ships.
  - Japan is such a special case that it needs far more development and probably its own setting material (Scott). These three versions are placeholders for that work.
- **Care.** The "fox-owning" families stigmatized in Izumo (an idea attested after 1668) still face prejudice, and Ainu religion is its own tradition.

> **Further in:** in the classics, the god Ōkuninushi withdrew from the visible world to rule "hidden matters." Dejima is the only door for Dutch ships. Nobody has said it's the only door.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The gnomon trials.** On 27–29 December the emperor sets the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest against Yang Guangxian to predict the noon shadow. In our history Verbiest wins, perhaps after adjusting his figures following the first day, and the Jesuits get the Bureau back.
- **The coast.** The clearance is in force; officials are petitioning to lift it. In our history it's lifted in 1669, and typhoons wreck the rebuilt houses.
- **Taiwan** stands. The south is quiet under its three generals.
- **The Daoists.** Wang Changyue is alive. Kangxi's Sacred Edict, "eliminate heterodox beliefs," is two years off.
- **Korea** is two years from famine, and its cattle are already dying.
- **Japan.** The north is close to war; in Edo, the rebuilding goes on.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The clerk.** A calendar clerk thrown out of the Bureau after the trials, with a sealing date in the records that doesn't add up.
- A minor Ming prince's sealed tomb, in a valley the new dynasty ignores.
- **A test.** A Mutapan curiosity reaches Beijing, and an emperor who tests claims wants to test it.
- **The line.** A smuggler crossing the cleared coast to Taiwan.
- **A Wutong gift**, and what it costs a family.
- **A lost child** in a Japanese mountain village at dusk.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
North America in 1668 is a continent of Indigenous powers with European footholds on its edges. The epidemics came, but Wisdom medicine and divinity blunted each outbreak, enough to leave the east coast barely colonized. The power in front is the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, in the middle of the Beaver Wars. To the south, Spain holds the Mexican plateau, but one of the pantheons pushed back, and the Itza Maya at Nojpetén have kept Spain out for half a century. The Caribbean is turning into sugar.

**The one thing to remember:** the Europeans here are small. New France, New England and New York live on trade, treaties and permission, and the diplomacy that matters runs through Onondaga, not Quebec.

> **Further in:** in our history, many "empty" coastal lands were empty because their people had died a generation before the colonists came.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
None of this is wilderness. The eastern woodlands, the Plains and the Maya forest are worked land, and their owners are home.

- **The eastern woodlands.** Iroquoian towns are palisaded longhouse towns in cleared fields, moved every generation or so (unverified, standard figure). People burn the underbrush to open the woods.
- **The Three Sisters.** Maize, beans and squash in one hill, feeding more people than any of the three alone. Women own and work the fields.
- **The Great Lakes.** Five freshwater seas, routes by canoe. The beaver near Haudenosaunee country are trapped out; the fur front has moved west.
- **The Plains.** Foot hunters with dog travois, and farming towns on the rivers; horses are already spreading north. The Lakota are a woodland and wild-rice people around Mille Lacs, not yet the mounted nation of the Black Hills.
- **The Southwest.** The late 1660s are drought and famine years in New Mexico (unverified).
- **The Mexican plateau.** Mexico City flooded in 1629 and stayed under water for about five years; the drainage works are still being dug.
- **The Maya lowlands.** What outsiders call jungle is a managed forest garden, cycled through milpa and fallow.
- **The Caribbean.** Trade winds all year, hurricanes June to November. Barbados is cleared for cane; yellow fever arrived with the slave ships in 1647 (unverified).
- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age; colonial records describe hard winters (unverified for specific years).

> *"The French call it the wilderness. They mean they don't know whose it is. Ask, and someone will tell you."* (a Mohawk trader at Albany)

> **Further in:** the 1616–19 epidemic emptied Patuxet, and Plymouth was built on its site. Here that epidemic was tempered, not stopped.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Haudenosaunee.** Five Nations (Seneca, Cayuga, Oneida, Onondaga, Mohawk) under the Great Law of Peace. A Grand Council of 50 chiefs, with the Onondaga as Firekeepers, decides by consensus. **Clan Mothers choose the chiefs and can remove them.** With Dutch guns they dispersed the Wendat in 1648–49 and defeated the Erie, and they take captives to replace their dead.
- **Their neighbors.** The Anishinaabe and Cree around the upper lakes; the Mi'kmaq of the east coast, with their own Grand Council and an alliance with France; the Wendat survivors; the Powhatan's paramount chiefdom in tidewater Virginia, which in our history was confined to reserved lands by 1646. Here too: history keeps its shape.
- **New France.** Quebec since 1608, royal since 1663. A company holds the fur monopoly. France's crown owns its church and absorbs magic, so New France's magic is presumably licensed from Paris.
- **The English.** New York (Dutch until 1664), Virginia, New England, Barbados and Jamaica. Some of the Agitators' sympathizers run these colonies.
- **New Spain.** Spain's state is Church-run and regulates magic. Nahua towns keep their own councils; Tlaxcala, which allied with Cortés, won privileges for it. The Maya. The Itza still hold their island city of Nojpetén in Petén, as they did in our history until 1697, and here their gods' answer is why the friars keep failing.
- **Nojpetén.** The Itza capital on an island in Lake Petén Itzá, under a king titled *Aj Kan Ek'*, "serpent star." The Itza expelled the friars, wiped out a Spanish force in 1624, and have had no contact with Spain since. Their prophecy says it isn't yet time to convert.
- **The Pueblos.** Under Spanish rule, which burns kivas and bans Pueblo people from owning horses and guns.
- **Every empire has its conquered.** The Confederacy absorbed its captives; the Mexica had their tributaries, and Tlaxcala remembers.

> **Further in:** in 1675, in our history, New Mexico's governor arrested 47 Pueblo religious leaders for sorcery. Here, sorcery is real.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Indigenous North America has the same buff the Inca had: Wisdom medicine and divinity. Healers, druids and clerics are rare, so they soften an epidemic and can't cancel it, but softened is the difference between a nation and a remnant. It's why the continent isn't a European one.

**The catch:** someone cured by magic never gains immunity, while survivors of the slow way do, so every healed town is exposed again when the sickness comes back.

- **Medicine as institutions.** The Haudenosaunee have medicine societies with members, songs and obligations. Their rites are private: the Confederacy asks that the masks not be shown, and the book doesn't depict them.
- **Knowledge is universal.** The Three Sisters is agronomy; fire is land management. A Nahua physician wrote an illustrated herbal at Tlatelolco in 1552; the Maya codices hold eclipse and Venus tables.
- **The shaking tent.** A specialist calls spirits into a small lodge after dark to see distant events and find lost things. Europe's crowned heads talk through shewstones.
- **Being called.** Young people fast alone for a guardian in a dream. Scott's Lakota druid takes buffalo form; in 1668 her people hunt bison on foot at the prairie edge. She stays in 1668, at the prairie edge, as written. (Lakota ceremony isn't depicted.)
- **Mesoamerica.** The *tonalli* is a soul a fright can knock loose; a *nahualli* is a companion animal, or a person who becomes one.
- **The missions.** Before Lanternhall, the Church's healing was the only kind Europe trusted, and its price was conversion. Here, Indigenous medicine works too, which takes the lever away.

> **Further in:** in 1634 a Jesuit watched an Innu shaking-tent specialist, Carigouan, at work. In the Peacemaker's story, Tadodaho, an Onondaga sorcerer with snakes in his hair, was straightened, not killed, and his title still chairs the Grand Council (detail unverified).

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
North America's Hidden are many peoples' Hidden, not one. Nearly everything written about them was recorded between 1880 and 1930. These are living traditions.

- **The Jogah** (Haudenosaunee). Little people of caves and stream banks who call humans "our grandchildren." Drumming with no drummer means they want tobacco. They warn and enrich the respectful and sicken the neglectful. Stories about them are told only in winter.
- **The Yunwi Tsunsdi and the Nunnehi** (Cherokee). Knee-high drummers who lead lost children home, and a rule: "Little People, I want to take this." The Nunnehi look like anyone else and keep townhouses under the bald mountains; a boy who visited one came back to be told there was no house there.
- **The memegwesi** (Anishinaabe and Cree). Small, hairy-faced beings in the cliff cracks over the water, linked to the red ochre paintings.
- **The wendigo** (Cree *wīhtikōw*, Ojibwe *wiindigoo*). It is what a person becomes when hunger breaks the duty to share, not a horror monster, and many people don't speak of it lightly. Use it with care or not at all.
- **The owners of springs** (Gulf Coast Nahua). Chaneques seize a person's *tonal* by fright near water and are never called by their real names. The Maya *aluxes* guard a field for seven years; they're attested for 1668 only by inference.
- **The dead without navels** (Taíno). The *opía* come out at night to eat guava; you can tell them by the missing navel. Recorded in the 1490s, they are the earliest record here.
- **The edge of the village.** It half fits. Iroquoian towns have palisades and fields with edges, but the beings past them are kin, inside the reciprocity the Thanksgiving Address names, not civilization's enemy. From Quebec, though, the "fringe where the Hidden live" is someone else's home. The Hidden Killers patrol the colonies' villages, where the edge is a palisade against the woods; each nation keeps its own protectors on its own terms. The Wild Hunt rides here too.

> **Further in:** Cherokee tradition says the Nunnehi fought for the Cherokee against their enemies at Nikwasi.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The Beaver Wars** go on, moving west. The Dutch who sold the guns are gone.
- **Hudson Bay.** Radisson and des Groseilliers' first voyage for the English sails this year; only des Groseilliers' ship gets through.
- **New Mexico** is in drought, famine and Apache raids.
- **Nojpetén** stands. In our history it falls in 1697.
- **The Caribbean.** Barbados runs on slaves under an English slave code. The Maroons hold Jamaica's mountains. Dominica and St Vincent are reserved for the Kalinago.
- **The strange metal.** Every power is hunting for what runs Mutapa's devices, and Spain sits on it in the Chocó. A fleet bound there would water in the Caribbean.

> **Further in:** horses were moving north along Indigenous trade routes long before Santa Fe noticed.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The guns.** With the Dutch gone, who arms the Confederacy, and what do they want for it?
- **The kivas.** A governor's sorcery charges, and a Tewa religious leader named Po'pay. Whether the Pueblos rise, and when, is the table's.
- **The fleet in Port Royal.** An English squadron asking how well Spain holds New Granada.
- **The mission's price.** A Jesuit healer, a dying village, and a medicine society that can do it for free.
- **Not yet time.** An Itza priest reading the prophecy, and a Spanish road being surveyed toward the lake.

sections.heading: Playing Here
At a Glance
sections.text:
South America is the war that didn't end. In our history the Inca state fell with Vilcabamba in 1572. Here the huacas rose, and the conquest became a standing war. Spain holds the coast and the lowlands, the Inca hold the high ground, and Potosí, Spain's silver mountain, is the frontier between them. In 1668 the world's powers have just realized that Spain is also sitting on platina in the Chocó, the metal Mutapa runs on, and has been throwing it in the river.
